pub fn try_listen_tls_on(addr: text, port: integer, cert: text, key: text) -> Server
api.doc:
TLS on a chosen bind address — `listen_tls` + `listen_on` combined. An empty `addr` means
`0.0.0.0`.

api.sig: pub fn bound(self: Server) -> boolean
api.doc:
True when this server actually owns its port.  Always true for a `listen()` result
(that halts otherwise) — it is the check that makes a `try_listen()` result usable.

api.sig: pub fn next_nonblocking(self: Server) -> Request
api.doc:
Non-blocking variant of `next()`.  Returns null immediately if no
connection is pending.  Use this when the server interleaves HTTP
accept with multi-client WS polling on a single port (single_port
audience demo / future TTT-style multi-tab apps).

api.sig: pub fn next(self: Server) -> Request
pub fn respond(self: Request, status: integer, body: text)
pub fn respond_typed(self: Request, status: integer, body: text, content_type: text)
pub fn respond_bytes(self: Request, status: integer, body: vector<u8>, content_type: text)
api.doc:
Send a response whose body is RAW BYTES — an image, a font, a wasm module, any
payload that is not text.

⚠⚠ USE THIS FOR ANYTHING BINARY; the text responses cannot carry it and FAIL SILENTLY.
`respond`/`respond_typed` take loft `text`, and a `text` built from non-UTF-8 bytes is
the EMPTY text (`text_from_bytes` documents exactly that). So serving a PNG through
them answers **200 OK with Content-Length: 0** — a success the caller cannot
distinguish from an empty file, and a broken image with no error anywhere. Measured
2026-08-21: the loft review viewer had been serving every `doc/images/*.png` that way.

`content_type` empty defaults to `application/octet-stream`, which is the honest
answer for bytes of unknown kind — name the real type when you know it
(`image/png`, `font/woff2`, `application/wasm`).

api.sig: pub fn header(self: Request, name: text) -> text
api.doc:
Look up a request header case-insensitively (e.g. "Range", "Origin",
"If-None-Match"); returns "" if absent. Values containing ':' (an Origin URL,
a date) are rejoined intact.
Example: @SRV-002 — why a hand-rolled `h.split(':')[1]` over `headers` loses the port.

api.sig: pub fn respond_with_headers(self: Request, status: integer, body: text, headers: vector<text>)
api.doc:
Send a response with caller-controlled headers (Content-Range, ETag, the CORS
headers, …). `headers` is a vector of "Key: Value" lines; Content-Length is
auto-added from the body unless a header supplies one; the body is written
verbatim (binary-safe).

api.sig: pub fn cors_headers(origin: text) -> vector<text>
api.doc:
Standard CORS headers so a browser client can read Content-Range /
Content-Length / ETag on a cross-origin byte-range fetch. `origin` is the
allowed origin ("*" for any).

api.sig: pub fn serve_range(self: Request, body: text, extra: vector<text>) -> boolean
api.doc:
Serve a byte range of `body` when the request carries a Range header, adding
`extra` headers (CORS / ETag) to the 206 or 416. Returns true if a range
response was sent; false when there is no Range header (the caller serves the
full body). Single-range "bytes=off-last" / open-ended "bytes=off-" only.
Example: @SRV-003 — the boolean says WHO answered; false is the case you must handle.

api.sig: pub fn serve_data(self: Request, body: text, etag: text, origin: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
One-call helper to serve a (possibly binary) resource with full byte-range +
CORS + HEAD + conditional support — the server counterpart to the web client's
http_get_range / http_size. `etag` "" skips conditional; `origin` "" skips CORS.
Example: @SRV-003 — this one takes every branch, so it is always true and always final.

api.sig: pub fn respond_html(self: Request, body: text)
api.doc: Convenience wrappers for the common cases TTT v3 needs.

api.sig: pub fn respond_css(self: Request, body: text)
pub fn respond_js(self: Request, body: text)
pub fn respond_loft(self: Request, body: text)
pub fn respond_404(self: Request)

pub fn ws_upgrade() -> WebSocket
pub fn next(self: WebSocket) -> text?
pub fn send(self: WebSocket, msg: text) -> boolean
pub fn send_binary(self: WebSocket, msg: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
Send `msg` as a binary WebSocket frame (opcode 2).  Loft
`text` is a byte buffer — pack u8/u16/i32/etc. into it via
`to_bytes` style code, then ship it.

api.sig: pub fn last_opcode(self: WebSocket) -> integer
api.doc:
Opcode of the last frame returned by `next` on this socket.
Use after `next` to decide whether to interpret the payload
as utf-8 text or as a binary blob.

api.sig: pub fn close(self: WebSocket)
pub struct WsEvent
api.doc:
Event delivered to the on_event handler.  `connected` and
`message` are mutually-exclusive booleans for fast dispatch
without an integer enum.  Wire format `<msg_id>:<payload>`
is parsed by `run` so msg_id and payload come pre-split.

api.sig: pub fn run(self: Server, on_event: fn(WsEvent))
api.doc:
Block forever, draining events and calling the handler.
Malformed message frames are logged at warn level and silently
dropped — the handler never sees them.

api.sig: pub fn poll_event(self: Server) -> WsEvent
api.doc:
Non-blocking single-event drain — returns the next WsEvent, or null
when nothing is pending.  Lets a server that also needs a periodic
tick (timers, decay, snapshots) run its OWN loop while still using the
efficient Rust-side event pump: drain `poll_event` in a batch, do the
periodic work, idle-sleep when a pass produced nothing.  `run` above is
the convenience wrapper for servers that only react to events.

Disconnect (kind 2) and malformed message frames are skipped internally
(the caller never sees them), so a null return always means "idle".

api.sig: pub fn respond_html(self: Server, body: text)
api.doc:
Reply to the HTTP request currently parked by a `http` WsEvent and
close it.  Call exactly once from the handler for an `ev.http` event.

api.doc: Send a frame to a specific client.  Returns true on success.

api.sig: pub fn broadcast(self: Server, msg: text) -> integer
api.doc:
Send a frame to every active client.  Returns the count of
successful sends.  Iteration happens entirely in Rust.

api.sig: pub fn disconnect(self: Server, client_id: integer)
api.doc:
Forcefully close one client's connection.  The slot is freed
for reuse by future accepts.

random.description: Pseudo-random number generation — PCG-64 thread-local PRNG with rand_seed reproducibility.

api.sig: pub fn rand(lo: integer, hi: integer) -> integer?
api.doc:
Returns a random integer in [lo, hi] (inclusive).
Returns null when lo > hi or when either argument is null.

api.sig: pub fn rand_seed(seed: integer)
api.doc:
Seeds the thread-local random number generator with the given value.
Call this before rand() or rand_indices() to get reproducible sequences.

api.sig: pub fn rand_indices(n: integer) -> vector<integer>
api.doc:
Returns a vector of n integers [0, 1, ..., n-1] in a random order.
Useful for random iteration, shuffling, or sampling without replacement.
Returns an empty vector when n is 0 or null.

api.sig: pub struct RandStream
pub fn seed_stream(seed: integer) -> RandStream
api.doc:
Seed an independent stream. Any integer seed is valid (negative and zero included);
equal seeds give equal streams, different seeds give decorrelated streams.

api.sig: pub fn get(self: RandStream, lo: integer, hi: integer) -> integer?
api.doc:
A random integer in [lo, hi] (inclusive) from THIS stream, advancing it.
Returns null when lo > hi (the same contract as the global rand()).

api.sig: pub fn indices(self: RandStream, n: integer) -> vector<integer>
api.doc:
A random permutation of [0, 1, ..., n-1] from THIS stream (Fisher-Yates), advancing
it. Empty when n is 0, negative or null (the same contract as rand_indices()).

api.sig: pub fn rand(lo: integer, hi: integer) -> integer?
api.doc:
Returns a random integer in [lo, hi] (inclusive).
Returns null when lo > hi or when either argument is null.
Draws from the ONE hidden generator every call site shares — see `rand_seed`.
Example: @RND-001 — why a seeded global sequence is not yours, and what a
RandStream gives instead.

api.sig: pub fn rand_seed(seed: integer)
api.doc:
Seeds the thread-local random number generator with the given value.
Call this before rand() or rand_indices() to get reproducible sequences — but
note that it fixes what the GENERATOR produces, not what you receive: it is
shared, so one `rand()` from anywhere else shifts everything after it.  When
reproducibility is a requirement rather than a convenience, own a stream.
Example: @RND-001 — a foreign draw between two of yours, and the same
interruption against a RandStream.

api.sig: pub fn rand_indices(n: integer) -> vector<integer>
api.doc:
Returns a vector of n integers [0, 1, ..., n-1] in a random order.
Useful for random iteration, shuffling, or sampling without replacement.
Returns an empty vector when n is 0 or null.
Example: @RND-001 — this draws from the shared global generator too.

api.sig: pub struct RandStream
pub fn seed_stream(seed: integer) -> RandStream
api.doc:
Seed an independent stream. Any integer seed is valid (negative and zero included);
equal seeds give equal streams, different seeds give decorrelated streams.
Example: @RND-001 — the reason to prefer this over `rand_seed`.
Example: @RND-003 — equal seeds replay exactly, so a recorded seed is a
recorded run.

api.sig: pub fn get(self: RandStream, lo: integer, hi: integer) -> integer?
api.doc:
A random integer in [lo, hi] (inclusive) from THIS stream, advancing it.
Returns null when lo > hi (the same contract as the global rand()).
Example: @RND-002 — assigning a stream COPIES it, passing one to a function
LINKS it, so a helper that draws spends the caller's sequence.

api.sig: pub fn indices(self: RandStream, n: integer) -> vector<integer>
api.doc:
A random permutation of [0, 1, ..., n-1] from THIS stream (Fisher-Yates), advancing
it by exactly n - 1 draws. Empty when n is 0, negative or null (the same contract
as rand_indices()).
Example: @RND-003 — a shuffle is a countable number of draws, so inserting one
shifts the rest of the sequence by a known amount rather than adding noise.

regex.description: Small-script regex: matches / find / split / match_groups / replace, with a thread-local pattern cache.

api.sig: pub fn find(pattern: text, input: text) -> integer
api.doc:
Byte offset of the first match of `pattern` in `input`, or null when
there is no match (or the pattern is invalid).

api.sig: pub fn split(pattern: text, input: text) -> iterator<text>
api.doc:
Split `input` on matches of `pattern`, yielding each piece lazily through
an `iterator<text>` (reuses loft's coroutine channel — nothing is
materialised).

api.sig: pub fn matches(both: text, pattern: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
True if `pattern` matches anywhere in the text.  `both` registers this as
BOTH a method (`line.matches(p)`) and a free function (`matches(line, p)`).
`matches` keeps the bare name — it is collision-free on `text` (the stdlib
has `contains`, not `matches`) and reads as regex on its own.

api.sig: pub fn regex_find(self: text, pattern: text) -> integer
api.doc:
Byte offset of the first match of `pattern` in the text, or null.
Prefixed because bare `find` collides with stdlib `text.find` (literal
substring search).  Call as  line.regex_find("[0-9]+").

api.sig: pub fn regex_split(self: text, pattern: text) -> iterator<text>
api.doc:
Split the text on matches of `pattern`, yielding pieces lazily.  Prefixed
because bare `split` collides with stdlib `text.split` (character
separator).  Call as  for piece in line.regex_split("[,;]") { }.

api.sig: pub fn search(self: text, pattern: text) -> integer
api.doc:
Byte offset of the first match of `pattern` in the text, or null when there
is no match (or the pattern is invalid).  The conventional regex-search verb
— named `search`, not `find`, because bare `find` on text is the stdlib's
literal substring search.  Call as  line.search("[0-9]+").
Example: @RGX-001 — why this is `search` and not `find`, and what a bare
`find(pattern, input)` answers instead.
Example: @RGX-002 — the answer is a BYTE offset (slice with it, compare it to
`size()` not `len()`), and a miss is null despite the `integer` return type.

api.sig: pub fn matches(both: text, pattern: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
True if `pattern` matches anywhere in the text.  `both` registers this as
BOTH a method (`line.matches(p)`) and a free function (`matches(line, p)`).
Collision-free on `text` (the stdlib has `contains`, not `matches`).
Example: @RGX-003 — a pattern that never compiled answers false, exactly like
text that simply did not match.

api.sig: pub fn split_on(self: text, pattern: text) -> iterator<text>
api.doc:
Split the text on matches of `pattern`, yielding each piece lazily through
an `iterator<text>` (reuses loft's coroutine channel — nothing is
materialised).  Named `split_on`, not `split`, because bare `split` on text
is the stdlib character-separator split.  Call as
for piece in line.split_on("[,;]") { }.
Example: @RGX-004 — it yields the gaps between matches, so a separator at
either end leaves an empty piece and unmatched text comes back as ONE piece.

api.sig: pub fn find(pattern: text, input: text) -> integer
api.doc:
Example: @RGX-001 — reachable only as `regex::find`; the bare spelling
resolves the stdlib `text` method and answers something else entirely.

api.sig: pub fn split(pattern: text, input: text) -> iterator<text>
api.doc:
Example: @RGX-001 — same shadow as `find`: bare `split` is the stdlib's
character split, not this one.

pub fn regex_split(self: text, pattern: text) -> iterator<text>

hex_grid.description: Hex-grid geometry — axial/pixel conversion, neighbours, distance, and corner offsets.

hex_terrain.description: The OVERLAND terrain layer of the `hex_*` family: a coarse overland hex lattice

api.sig: pub struct TerrainType
api.doc:
One terrain type = content (a bundle row in the consuming game).
tt_rise and tt_steep are INDEPENDENT; tt_wet marks water bodies (sea/lake):
they take no relief and no boundary contest.

api.sig: pub struct TerrainParams
api.doc:
Algorithm parameters (engine side).  terrain_params() gives the blueprint's
user-tuned defaults; every field is meters unless noted.

api.sig: pub fn terrain_params(seed: integer, tile: float) -> TerrainParams
pub struct Terrain
api.doc: Parallel per-cell vectors, index = r * tr_nx + c (odd-r offset coords).

api.sig: pub fn terrain_new(nx: integer, ny: integer) -> Terrain
pub fn terrain_idx(t: Terrain, c: integer, r: integer) -> integer
pub fn terrain_center(p: TerrainParams, c: integer, r: integer) -> (float, float)
api.doc:
Cell center in world meters — hex_grid's odd-r lattice scaled so the
horizontal pitch equals tp_tile (hex_grid's unit pitch is SQRT3).

api.sig: pub fn terrain_flow_to(t: Terrain, c: integer, r: integer) -> (integer, integer)
api.doc: The downstream cell of (c, r) — itself when it has no flow direction.

api.sig: pub fn terrain_hash01(seed: integer, ix: integer, iy: integer, ch: integer) -> float
pub fn terrain_vnoise(seed: integer, x: float, y: float, wl: float, ch: integer) -> float
pub fn terrain_fbm(seed: integer, x: float, y: float, wl0: float, octaves: integer, ch: integer) -> float
api.doc: Fractal sum, roughly in [-1, 1].

api.sig: pub fn terrain_detail_at(p: TerrainParams, x: float, y: float) -> float
api.doc:
Detail noise with DOMAIN WARP (the sampling space is swirled by a second
noise so the value-noise lattice never reads as a repeating pattern).

api.sig: pub fn terrain_ridge_at(p: TerrainParams, x: float, y: float) -> float
api.doc:
LOW-frequency ridged field, crest-sharpened: roughly ONE combined crest per
steep zone — peaks consolidate into ridgelines instead of speckling.

api.sig: pub fn terrain_hydrology(t: Terrain, p: TerrainParams, lake_mat: integer)
api.doc:
PRIORITY-FLOOD pit fill + steepest-descent flow + accumulation.  After this
every land cell drains to the sea; cells the flood raised by more than
tp_lake_fill become lakes (material set to lake_mat).  Selection-based
flood (O(n^2)) — overland grids are small and this runs once at gen time.

api.sig: pub fn terrain_relief_pass(t: Terrain, types: vector<TerrainType>, p: TerrainParams)
api.doc:
Wet flags + the compounded neighbor relief.  Call AFTER the caller has
classified land materials (relief reads the final wet set).

api.sig: pub struct TerrainSurf
api.doc: One blended surface record at a fine point.

api.sig: pub fn terrain_surface_at(t: Terrain, types: vector<TerrainType>, p: TerrainParams, x: float, y: float) -> TerrainSurf
api.doc:
Smooth kernel blend of the overland cells around (x, y) + the boundary-line
contest + the fine height.  Pure function — THE seam invariant lives here.

api.sig: pub fn terrain_blend_h(t: Terrain, p: TerrainParams, x: float, y: float) -> float
api.doc: Lightweight coarse-blend height only (for slopes along river courses).

api.sig: pub fn terrain_lake_field(p: TerrainParams, x: float, y: float, lakey: float) -> float
api.doc: The fractally jittered lake contour field (>= 0.5 = lake water).

api.sig: pub fn terrain_water_at(t: Terrain, types: vector<TerrainType>, p: TerrainParams, x: float, y: float) -> boolean
api.doc:
Is (x, y) open water (sea by the fine height contour, or lake)?  PRE-carve —
this is the shoreline rivers attach to.

api.sig: pub struct TerrainRiver
api.doc:
One river course PIECE: fine polyline (ends ON the shorelines) with
per-vertex water width, carve depth and valley falloff width.

api.sig: pub fn terrain_edge_cross(p: TerrainParams, ca: integer, ra: integer, cb: integer, rb: integer) -> (float, float)
api.doc:
THE EDGE BIT (user rule): a river never exits mid-side; each shared edge
carries one canonical left/right bit.  Both tiles hash the SORTED cell pair,
so they derive the same crossing point — seamless.

api.sig: pub fn terrain_control_pt(p: TerrainParams, c: integer, r: integer) -> (float, float)
api.doc:
The interior routing point of a tile (hash-jittered off-center; the natural
confluence spot — tributaries entering the tile share it).

api.sig: pub fn terrain_rivers(t: Terrain, types: vector<TerrainType>, p: TerrainParams) -> vector<TerrainRiver>
api.doc:
All river course pieces, fully shaped: anchors (edge bits + control points)
-> fractal displacement -> corner-cut smoothing -> shoreline trim -> width/
depth/valley-width per vertex (slope-shaped + the estuary depth bonus).

api.sig: pub struct TerrainSample
pub fn terrain_sample(t: Terrain, types: vector<TerrainType>, p: TerrainParams, rivers: vector<TerrainRiver>, x: float, y: float) -> TerrainSample
api.doc:
The full sample: surface + ADDITIVE valley carving from every course near
the point + the water classification (sea floods the carved mouth).  Pure
function of (t, types, p, rivers, x, y) — THE window-independence invariant.

hex_world.description: Sparse 32x32-chunk hex-grid world data model — Cell / Chunk / World with binary save/load.

api.sig: pub struct Cell
api.doc:
4-byte cell.  c_color uses the u8 typedef (integer limit(0,255)
size(1)); c_age uses u16 (size(2)).  Storage packs to exactly 4
bytes per cell — the projector ships them through the binary
surface in chunk-major order.

c_color = 0 means "empty" (no crystal, no TTT mark).  Both clients
treat 0 as background; non-zero as live content.

api.sig: pub struct Chunk
api.doc:
32x32 grid at chunk coords (ck_cx, ck_cz).  Index into ck_cells:
hx * 32 + hz where hx, hz ∈ [0, 31].  Same shape as moros_map's
Chunk minus the cy layer (this world is single-layer).

api.sig: pub struct World
api.doc:
Top-level container.  Sparse: only chunks with at least one
non-empty cell live in `chunks`; empty chunks are removed by the
tick loop's GC pass.  `tick` is monotonic per server lifetime.

api.sig: pub fn chunk_idx_32(v: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
floor(v / 32) — handles negative v correctly (C-style `/` rounds
toward zero, which silently maps cell (-1, 0) to chunk 0 instead
of chunk -1).

api.sig: pub fn hex_idx_32(v: integer) -> integer
api.doc: v mod 32, always in [0, 31].

api.sig: pub fn cell_empty() -> Cell
api.doc:
Default empty cell.  All fields zero; serialises to four 0x00
bytes on the wire.

api.sig: pub fn build_chunk(cx: integer, cz: integer) -> Chunk
api.doc:
Build a 32x32 chunk filled with empty cells at chunk coords
(cx, cz).

api.sig: pub fn world_empty() -> World
api.doc: New empty world, tick 0, no chunks.

api.sig: pub fn has_chunk(self: World, q: integer, r: integer) -> boolean
api.doc: True iff a chunk exists at the global (q, r).

api.sig: pub fn ensure_chunk(self: &World, q: integer, r: integer)
api.doc:
Ensure a chunk exists at the global (q, r); creates a 32x32 of
empty cells if absent.

api.sig: pub fn get_cell(self: World, q: integer, r: integer) -> Cell
api.doc:
Read the cell at global (q, r).  Returns `cell_empty()` when the
chunk does not exist (sparse-world convention — empty chunks are
implicitly all-empty).

api.sig: pub fn set_cell(self: &World, q: integer, r: integer, value: Cell)
api.doc:
Write a cell at global (q, r).  Creates the containing chunk on
demand; does NOT GC empty chunks (the tick loop's end-of-tick
pass owns that).

api.sig: pub fn cell_count(self: World) -> integer
api.doc: Total number of non-empty cells across every chunk.

api.sig: pub fn neighbour_count(self: World, q: integer, r: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Count filled axial-hex neighbours of the cell at global (q, r).
Returns 0..=6.  Empty centre cell is fine — neighbours are read
independently of the centre's state.

api.sig: pub fn tick_and_decay(self: &World, base_lifetime: integer,
api.doc:
── Tick + decay ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

One world step: advances `tick`, ages every non-empty cell by 1,
then removes any cell whose `c_age` has crossed
`effective_lifetime + decay_window` where
`effective_lifetime = base_lifetime + neighbour_lease *
filled_neighbour_count`.  Neighbour counts are computed against
the PRE-TICK state — a single tick can remove a connected blob
of cells, but the cascade (centre losing its neighbour support)
only fires on the NEXT tick.  This keeps the simulation
deterministic per-step and prevents one-tick complete collapse
of large clusters.

api.sig: pub fn world_save(self: World, path: text)
api.doc: Save the world to `path`, replacing whatever was there.

api.sig: pub fn world_load(self: &World, path: text) -> integer
api.doc:
Load the world from `path`.  Mutates `self` in place; pre-existing
cells in `self` are left untouched unless the snapshot overwrites
the same (q, r).  Returns the number of cells loaded.  Returns 0 if
the file does not exist, has the wrong magic, or carries an
unsupported version — never panics.

input.description: Game input for loft — action/axis bindings resolved to per-tick input state.

api.sig: pub struct ActionBinding
api.doc:
One named action: "jump" → [KEY_SPACE, KEY_UP] (any of the listed
keys triggers the action).  An empty `ab_keys` is degenerate but
valid — the action will simply never fire.

api.sig: pub struct AxisBinding
api.doc:
One named axis: pair of (negative key, positive key) → -1.0 / 0.0
/ +1.0.  If both are down simultaneously the axis reads 0.0 (they
cancel) — same convention as Unity / Godot's built-in axis pairs.

api.sig: pub struct Bindings
api.doc:
Full binding set — game code constructs this once and passes it
into `input_new`.  Re-binding at runtime: mutate this struct in
place (or build a new one) and call `input_set_bindings`.

api.sig: pub struct InputState
api.doc:
Abstract input state.  Fields are documented but considered
opaque — query via the `is_action_*` / `get_axis` / `mouse_*`
functions below.

`is_keys_now[i]` is true if key code `i` is currently down;
`is_keys_prev[i]` holds the same flag from the previous tick so
edge detection compares the two.  Mouse buttons are a bitmask
(`MB_LEFT | MB_RIGHT | …`).

api.sig: pub fn input_new(b: Bindings) -> InputState
api.doc:
Construct an `InputState` from a `Bindings` set.  Both key tables
start fully released; the first call to `input_tick` populates
`is_keys_now` (and `is_keys_prev` stays all-false, so any key down
on the first tick fires its `just_pressed` edge — the documented
"first frame counts as a transition" semantics).

api.sig: pub fn input_set_bindings(self: &InputState, b: Bindings)
api.doc:
Replace the binding set on a live state (e.g. after the player
remaps keys in a settings menu).  Does NOT clear the key tables —
in-flight key presses survive the rebind so a remap doesn't
strand an already-held key.

api.sig: pub fn input_tick(self: &InputState)
api.doc:
Poll the graphics input primitives and refresh state for one tick.
Reads `gl_key_pressed` for every key code referenced by the
current bindings (avoids a 256-call sweep — only ask about keys
the game actually cares about), plus `gl_mouse_x`/`gl_mouse_y`/
`gl_mouse_button`/`gl_mouse_wheel` unconditionally.

api.sig: pub fn input_tick_from_state(
api.doc:
Advance state from a caller-supplied snapshot instead of polling
`graphics`.  Used by tests (no GL context) and by network replay
/ record-playback systems.  `keys` length is clamped to KEY_MAX;
out-of-range entries are ignored.

api.sig: pub fn is_action_pressed(self: const InputState, action: text) -> boolean
api.doc: True if ANY of the action's bound keys is currently down.

api.sig: pub fn is_action_just_pressed(self: const InputState, action: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
True for exactly one tick: the moment any of the action's bound
keys transitions from up to down.  If multiple bound keys all
transition on the same tick it still fires once.

api.sig: pub fn is_action_just_released(self: const InputState, action: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
True for exactly one tick: the moment any of the action's bound
keys transitions from down to up.

api.sig: pub fn get_axis(self: const InputState, axis: text) -> float
api.doc:
Read an axis pair: -1.0 if only `ax_neg` is down, +1.0 if only
`ax_pos` is down, 0.0 if neither or both.  Unknown axis name
returns 0.0.

api.sig: pub fn mouse_x(self: const InputState) -> float
api.doc:
Mouse position — pixels from the top-left of the window
(matches `graphics::gl_mouse_x` / `gl_mouse_y`).

api.sig: pub fn mouse_y(self: const InputState) -> float
pub fn mouse_button_down(self: const InputState, button: integer) -> boolean
api.doc:
True if the given mouse button (`MB_LEFT` / `MB_RIGHT` / `MB_MIDDLE`)
is currently down.  Pass the constant, not a bitmask of multiple.

api.sig: pub fn mouse_button_just_pressed(self: const InputState, button: integer) -> boolean
api.doc:
True for exactly one tick — the moment the button transitions
from up to down.

api.sig: pub fn mouse_button_just_released(self: const InputState, button: integer) -> boolean
api.doc:
True for exactly one tick — the moment the button transitions
from down to up.

api.sig: pub fn mouse_wheel(self: const InputState) -> integer
api.doc:
Accumulated scroll-wheel delta since the last `input_tick` —
positive = scroll up.  Mirrors `graphics::gl_mouse_wheel`.

ssh.description: SSH client for loft — drive an interactive remote shell (e.g. attach tmux) over password auth, never stored. Native-only.

api.sig: pub struct Session
api.doc:
A live SSH session.  `handle >= 0` once the TCP connect + transport handshake
succeed; `< 0` means the connect failed.  Obtain one from `connect`.

api.sig: pub fn byte_at(idx: integer, data: text) -> integer
api.doc:
Read the byte at `idx` (0..size) of a `recv` result.  A terminal stream is raw
bytes, so read it byte-by-byte rather than as UTF-8.  Out of range returns -1 —
not 0, which the stream itself may legitimately carry.
Example: @SSH-002 — bound the loop with `size`, and test the end with `< 0`.

api.sig: pub fn connect(host: text, port: integer) -> Session
api.doc:
Open a TCP connection to `host:port` and run the SSH transport handshake.
Check `ok()` before authenticating.
Example: @SSH-001 — a failed session stays callable and silent, so `ok()` is the
only thing that reports it.

api.sig: pub fn ok(self: Session) -> boolean
api.doc:
True when the session connected and completed the transport handshake.
Example: @SSH-001 — skip this and the whole session ladder runs, quietly, on nothing.

api.sig: pub fn login(self: Session, user: text, password: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
Authenticate with a password.  Returns true on success.  The password is used
only for this handshake and is never stored by the library.

api.sig: pub fn open_shell(self: Session, term: text, cols: integer, rows: integer) -> boolean
api.doc:
Request a pseudo-terminal of `cols` x `rows` (terminal type `term`, e.g.
"xterm-256color") and start the login shell.  Returns true on success.

api.sig: pub fn send(self: Session, data: text)
api.doc: Send bytes to the remote shell (keystrokes, escape sequences).  Binary-safe.

api.sig: pub fn recv(self: Session) -> text
api.doc:
Return the bytes the remote shell produced since the last call, or "" when
nothing is pending (non-blocking).  Binary-safe: iterate 0..size(result) and
read each byte with `byte_at` — `size` is the BYTE count, which is what
`byte_at` is indexed against; `len` counts characters and would truncate.
Example: @SSH-002 — the byte a `len`-bounded loop drops, and why -1 is not 0.

api.sig: pub fn resize(self: Session, cols: integer, rows: integer)
api.doc:
Tell the remote the terminal resized to `cols` x `rows` so it re-flows.  Call
after a zoom / rotate / window resize.

api.sig: pub fn is_open(self: Session) -> boolean
api.doc: True while the shell channel is open (the remote has not closed it).

api.sig: pub fn close(self: Session)
api.doc: Close the shell channel and disconnect.

api.sig: pub fn arc_fill(cq: integer, cr: integer, n24: integer, cells: HexSet) -> integer
api.doc:
Fill the disk of shell `n24` about (cq, cr): every cell whose 4·squared-distance is at most
`n24`.  Entirely integer — the comparison that decides membership never touches a float.

`n24` is a SHELL, not a radius.  Hand it a value no `(k,m)` realises and it draws the
shell below without a word — `arc_shells_upto` is the grid to snap to first.

Example: @HXS-001

api.sig: pub fn arc_shell_max(cells: HexSet, cq: integer, cr: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
The outermost shell actually occupied, measured about (cq, cr).  This is the recoverable radius
parameter — the largest `N` present, not the continuous radius that was authored.

Example: @HXS-001

api.sig: pub fn arc_is_disk(cells: HexSet, cq: integer, cr: integer) -> boolean
api.doc:
Is the set EXACTLY the disk of its own outermost shell about (cq, cr)?  A tower must be, and a
blob will not be — this is what stops an arbitrary round-ish region being read as an arc.

Example: @HXS-001
Example: @HXS-009

api.sig: pub fn arc_recover_centre(cells: HexSet) -> (integer, integer, boolean)
api.doc:
Recover the centre: the unique cell about which the set IS a disk.  Searched over the cells of
the set itself — a disk's centre is always one of its own cells — so this is O(cells²) and needs
no guess.  Returns `found = false` when the region is not a disk about any of them, which is the
R2 answer for a shape that is not an arc.

Example: @HXS-001

api.sig: pub fn arc_shells_upto(n24: integer) -> vector<integer>
api.doc:
The shells that actually exist out to `n24`, ascending — the admissible radius grid, i.e. `Sep`
made concrete.  A value of `N` that no `(k,m)` realises is not a shell and cannot be authored.

api.sig: pub fn arc_wedge_has(cq: integer, cr: integer, q: integer, r: integer,
api.doc:
Is cell (q,r) inside the angular wedge running CCW from ray `lo` up to ray `hi`, about centre
(cq,cr)?  The wedge must span less than 180°, so `lo` and `hi` bound one contiguous arc.

api.sig: pub fn arc_door_wedge(cells: HexSet, edges: EdgeSet, cq: integer, cr: integer,
api.doc:
Place a door on the wall: re-material every boundary edge whose inside cell lies in the wedge to

centre and shell, are untouched.  Returns the number of edges marked.  The arc analog of
`place_opening`.

api.sig: pub fn arc_door_edges(cells: HexSet, edges: EdgeSet, mat: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Recover the door: count the boundary edges carrying `mat`, each exactly once (only the inside
cell of a boundary edge is in the set, so iterating inside cells visits every boundary edge
once).  This is the R1 read of the feature straight off storage.

api.doc: Example: @HXS-006

api.sig: pub fn box_ring_out(cells: HexSet, ring: HexSet) -> integer
api.doc:
── THE THICK WALL — a castle, not a cottage ───────────────────────────────

A cottage wall is an EDGE: it costs no floor, and 27 cells of house stay 27 cells of
house. A castle wall is different in kind — it is GROUND, wide enough to stand and walk
on, with an inside and an outside. So it is a ring of whole CELLS, and the only question
is which side of the selection it takes.

`box_ring_out` puts it OUTSIDE: the user's selection is the courtyard, untouched, and the
wall is the ring of cells around it. This is the one that matches the editor's gesture —
what you select is what you get to keep.

Example: @HXS-007

api.sig: pub fn box_ring_in(cells: HexSet, ring: HexSet) -> integer
api.doc:
`box_ring_in` takes it from INSIDE instead: the outermost layer of the selection becomes
wall and the courtyard shrinks. Same ring, opposite side — a town wall drawn to a
surveyed outer boundary wants this one.

Example: @HXS-007

api.sig: pub fn flood_outside(wall: HexSet, out: HexSet)
api.doc:
── DOES THE WALL HOLD? ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A ring that looks closed and is not is the exact defect `SPEC` I3's control names — "2
components, 0 enclosed, yet still 12/12 equivariant". For a thick wall the honest test is
not to count cells but to try to WALK IN: flood the outside and see whether it reaches the
courtyard. One hole and it does.

Relaxation rather than a queue: the region is a box, so sweeping until nothing changes
terminates in at most its perimeter in passes, and it needs no auxiliary storage.

Example: @HXS-007

api.sig: pub fn leak_count(inner: HexSet, out: HexSet) -> integer
api.doc:
How many cells of `inner` the outside flood reached. Zero means the wall holds.

Example: @HXS-007

api.sig: pub fn line_hexes(x0: float, y0: float, x1: float, y1: float, cells: HexSet) -> integer
api.doc:
── A THICK LINE — the town wall that is not a box ─────────────────────────

Same wall, no enclosure: a run of cells one hex wide, for a curtain wall or a rampart.
The cells are those the segment passes THROUGH — a hex is on the line iff the segment
enters it — so the chain is connected by construction and exactly one cell wide.

Stepping is by a third of a cell, which cannot skip one: consecutive samples are 0.577 wu
apart at most while a hex is 1.732 wu across, so every cell the segment crosses is
sampled at least twice.

Example: @HXS-007

api.sig: pub fn set_connected(cells: HexSet) -> boolean
api.doc:
Is every cell of the set reachable from every other, stepping only within the set?
A wall with a gap is not a wall; this is what makes "one hex wide" mean a CHAIN.

CONNECTED IS NOT CLOSED.  A ring with one cell taken out is still one connected chain, so
this answers true on a wall you can walk straight through.  For an ENCLOSURE the verdict is
`flood_outside` + `leak_count`; this one is the contract for an open run.

Example: @HXS-007

pub fn wall_step_k(d24: integer) -> integer
pub fn wall_step_m(d24: integer) -> integer
pub fn wall_is_exact(d24: integer) -> boolean
api.doc:
An even d24 is one of the 12 exact headings; an odd one is an in-between.

Example: @HXS-002

api.sig: pub fn wall_new(d24: integer, ox: float, oy: float, half: float, mat: integer) -> Wall
api.doc: Example: @HXS-008

api.sig: pub fn wall_angle_nominal(d24: integer) -> float
api.doc:
The nominal angle of `d24` in degrees, and the angle its step actually points at.  The two
are EQUAL on every even d24 and differ by 1.1021 degrees on every odd one — the gate prints
both rather than hiding it.  (4.11 degrees was the pre-`N = 39` in-between; see the table.)

api.sig: pub fn wall_angle_actual(d24: integer) -> float
api.doc: Example: @HXS-002

api.sig: pub fn wall_offset_signed(w: Wall, px: float, py: float) -> float
api.doc:
── writing into the foxel — ALONG the wall, not ACROSS it (OD-12) ─────────

THE FIRST TRY MARKED THE WRONG EDGES.  The band model asked "does the wall's thin
rectangle overlap this hex edge?" — and the edges a thin band overlaps are the ones lying
ACROSS it, roughly perpendicular.  A due-east wall came out as a comb of vertical pickets
(`X28`), because a hex has edges on only three lines (30/90/150) and none runs east, so a
wall going east cannot BE a run of hex edges pointing east.

THE WALL IS A BOUNDARY, NOT A BAND.  A straight line divides the plane into two
half-planes.  The hex edges that lie ALONG the line are exactly the ones that SEPARATE a
cell on one side from a cell on the other — the boundary between the two half-planes, which
for any direction is a single connected chain, straight in the three edge directions and an
alternating wobble otherwise.  This is `housedraw::draw_walls`' own rule (an edge between an
inside cell and an outside one), applied to a half-plane instead of a filled region — so it
inherits `I3`'s "closed by construction, one wide" for free.

Signed perpendicular offset of a world point from the wall's centre line.  Positive on the
side the normal (-dy, dx) points to; the sign is all that matters for separation.

api.sig: pub fn wall_separates(w: Wall, cx: float, cy: float, nx: float, ny: float) -> boolean
pub fn hex_corner_x(q: integer, r: integer, c: integer) -> float
api.doc:
── THE EDGE TABLE IS hex_grid's, NOT OURS ─────────────────────────────────

`hex_grid` already owns the moros edge-wall model — it says so in the file: "walls live
on hex edges, stored on 3 canonical edges per hex (dirs 0,1,2); dirs 3,4,5 belong to the
neighbour".  So `hex_edge_corners(dir)` IS the map from a neighbour direction to the two
corners bounding that edge, and `moros_render::emit_hex_walls` emits exactly those corner
pairs (N = 5->0, NE = 0->1, SE = 1->2) for the three stored slots.

A PRIVATE CORNER CONVENTION IS A SILENT WRONG ANSWER.  This file first carried its own
table (corner 0 at 30 degrees) and paired edge `c` with `nb_q/nb_r(q, r, c)` — but
hex_field's direction order is [E, W, SE, SW, NE, NW] and hex_grid's is
[E, SE, SW, W, NW, NE], so five of the six edges were stored against the WRONG
neighbour.  Every gate stayed green: a consistently wrong edge is still written once,
still idempotent, still non-empty.  Only measuring the marks back against the geometry
caught it, which is why `wall_edge_gap` below is a gate and not a comment.

Corner `c` of the hex at (q,r), in world units — hex_grid's table, hex_grid's indices.

api.sig: pub fn hex_corner_y(q: integer, r: integer, c: integer) -> float
pub fn cell_x_w(q: integer, r: integer) -> float
api.doc:
Cell centre in world units.  hex_field's exact lattice and hex_grid's float world agree
term for term — k*sqrt(3)/2 = sqrt(3)*(q + (r&1)/2) and m/2 = 1.5r — so this is the
integer spelling of `hex_to_px`, not a second convention.

api.sig: pub fn cell_y_w(q: integer, r: integer) -> float
pub fn wall_edge_gap(q: integer, r: integer, dir: integer) -> float
api.doc:
THE CHECK THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT: how far the midpoint of edge `dir` sits from the
midpoint between the two cell centres it is supposed to separate.  Zero for every
direction, or the edge table and the neighbour table disagree.

Example: @HXS-004

api.sig: pub fn hex_corner_tri_a(q: integer, r: integer, ci: integer) -> integer
pub fn hex_corner_tri_b(q: integer, r: integer, ci: integer) -> integer
pub fn wall_write(w: Wall, edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
THE ROUTINE: draw the wall into the foxel's three wall slots per hex.

An edge is marked iff the wall's centre line SEPARATES its two owning cells, within the run.
`edge_set_mat` stores an edge once, under whichever cell owns it, so writing from both sides
is idempotent — which is what makes the three-slots-per-hex model hold.

api.sig: pub fn wall_along_max(w: Wall, edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
── READING THE CHAIN BACK: is it ALONG the wall, and is it ONE chain? ─────

These are the two properties that distinguish the fixed marking from the old picket comb,
and neither is visible in the perpendicular STRAY (a comb and a zigzag both swing ~1 hex off
the line).  They are what `tests/wall.loft` §6 asserts.

ALONG-NESS.  For a marked edge between cells C and N, the vector C->N is PERPENDICULAR to the
edge.  An edge lying ALONG the wall therefore has C->N pointing ACROSS the wall — a small
`|C->N . wall_dir|`.  The old picket marked edges lying ACROSS the wall, whose C->N pointed
ALONG it — `|C->N . wall_dir| ~ 1`.

⚠ THAT MAKES THE WORST `|dot|` A DISCRIMINATOR ON HALF THE DIRECTIONS ONLY.  On the twelve
EXACT headings it tops out at 0.5 (N = 3) or 0.866 (N = 1), and nothing reaches 0.9.  On the
twelve IN-BETWEEN ones it reads **0.97** on completely correct output: a shallow line has to
cross the vertical edge between two cells of the SAME row wherever it steps up, and that
edge's dot is `cos(13.9 deg)`.  Measured, 3 of a 25-edge run are above 0.9.  So this number
describes the WOBBLE; it does not deliver a verdict, and a gate that thresholds it flags a
correct in-between wall.

The verdict is the CHAIN property below — two degree-1 vertices, no branches — which is exact
and holds for all 24 directions.

Example: @HXS-004

api.sig: pub fn wall_chain_ends(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
ONE CHAIN.  The marked edges form a connected path iff, keyed by their shared hex vertices
(exact triangle-lattice integers), exactly two vertices have degree 1 (the ends) and none has
degree > 2.  A picket comb of k disjoint edges has 2k degree-1 vertices — so this separates a
chain from a comb with no tolerance.  Returns the number of degree-1 vertices (2 for a single
chain, 0 for empty, 4 after a break, 2k for a comb).

Example: @HXS-004

api.sig: pub fn wall_chain_branches(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
Any vertex where three or more marked edges meet — a branch, which a straight wall's boundary
never has.  Non-zero means the marking is not a simple path.

Example: @HXS-004

api.sig: pub fn tri_b(d24: integer) -> integer

The direction's `N`.  Only THREE values occur over the 24 — measured, not assumed.

pub fn commensurable(n1: integer, n2: integer) -> boolean

api.sig: pub fn wall_from_run(d24: integer, a0: integer, b0: integer, p: integer, mat: integer) -> Wall
api.doc:
Build a wall from an ADMISSIBLE run: anchor vertex (a0,b0) in triangle coords, `p` periods of
direction `d24`.  The principled constructor — endpoints are hex vertices and the run is legal
(`wall_run_ok`), so the boundary chain terminates cleanly at both ends.  Defined here, below
`tri_x`/`wall_end_a`, so their float returns are known at the call site (see the note by
`wall_write`).

api.sig: pub fn hex_scale_round(x: float, y: float) -> (integer, integer)
api.doc:
Nearest HEX-SCALE lattice point (vertex OR centre) to a world point, in triangle
coordinates.  The hex-scale lattice is spanned by e1 = (sqrt3/2, 1/2) and e2 = (0, 1),
which is (a,b) = (3i, 3j) — a triangular lattice of spacing 1 wu.

Example: @HXS-008

api.sig: pub fn wall_offset_of(w: Wall, px: float, py: float) -> float
api.doc:
── EVALUATING THE MARKS BACK TO THE MESH (crawler / moros' own rule) ───────

This is the second half of the round trip, and it is NOT ours to invent: moros already
evaluates the three wall slots to geometry in `moros_render::emit_hex_walls`, and the
rule is one line — a marked edge becomes the quad standing on the segment between its
two corners.  `hex_edge_corners` is that segment, so the mesh a marked field produces is
fully determined here with no renderer, no `Mesh`, no graphics import.

WHAT THAT MESH IS.  It is the SAWTOOTH — the chain of hex edges the band crossed — not
the straight line we drew.  That is the honest state of the round trip: the foxel stores
where the wall went, and recovering the straight line from it is `rebuild`'s job.  So
the measurement below is not "does the mesh equal the wall" (it cannot) but "how far
does the mesh stray from it", which is the quantity the recovery has to undo.

Perpendicular distance from (px,py) to the wall's infinite centre line.

api.doc:

Only edges whose midpoint lies within the run are measured — past the ends there is no

api.doc:

api.sig: pub fn wall_read_run(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer, wq: integer, hq: integer)
api.doc:
Recover the whole run: direction, anchor and period count, all exact integers.  One period of
`d24` displaces a run by `3·tri(d24)`, so the endpoint displacement pins both `d24` and `p`; the
answer is canonicalised to the end that gives `p > 0`.  `ok` is false when the marking is not a
single chain, or when no direction divides the displacement — an unreadable field is REFUSED, not
approximated (law **P4**).

WHAT IT CANNOT RECOVER IS THE ORIENTATION, because the field does not store one: A-to-B and
B-to-A mark the identical edges.  The answer is canonicalised to `p > 0`, so the direction
comes back as `d24` OR as `d24 + 12` with the other endpoint as the anchor — both naming the
same wall.  `read.d == d` is therefore the wrong round-trip assertion; compare the ENDPOINTS.

api.sig: pub fn box_ring_out(cells: HexSet, ring: HexSet) -> integer
api.doc:
── THE THICK WALL — a castle, not a cottage ───────────────────────────────

A cottage wall is an EDGE: it costs no floor, and 27 cells of house stay 27 cells of
house. A castle wall is different in kind — it is GROUND, wide enough to stand and walk
on, with an inside and an outside. So it is a ring of whole CELLS, and the only question
is which side of the selection it takes.

`box_ring_out` puts it OUTSIDE: the user's selection is the courtyard, untouched, and the
wall is the ring of cells around it. This is the one that matches the editor's gesture —
what you select is what you get to keep.

Example: @HXS-007

surveyed outer boundary wants this one.

api.sig: pub fn flood_outside(wall: HexSet, out: HexSet)
api.doc:
── DOES THE WALL HOLD? ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A ring that looks closed and is not is the exact defect `SPEC` I3's control names — "2
components, 0 enclosed, yet still 12/12 equivariant". For a thick wall the honest test is
not to count cells but to try to WALK IN: flood the outside and see whether it reaches the
courtyard. One hole and it does.

Relaxation rather than a queue: the region is a box, so sweeping until nothing changes
terminates in at most its perimeter in passes, and it needs no auxiliary storage.

api.sig: pub fn line_hexes(x0: float, y0: float, x1: float, y1: float, cells: HexSet) -> integer
api.doc:
── A THICK LINE — the town wall that is not a box ─────────────────────────

Same wall, no enclosure: a run of cells one hex wide, for a curtain wall or a rampart.
The cells are those the segment passes THROUGH — a hex is on the line iff the segment
enters it — so the chain is connected by construction and exactly one cell wide.

Stepping is by a third of a cell, which cannot skip one: consecutive samples are 0.577 wu
apart at most while a hex is 1.732 wu across, so every cell the segment crosses is
sampled at least twice.

api.doc:
Is every cell of the set reachable from every other, stepping only within the set?
A wall with a gap is not a wall; this is what makes "one hex wide" mean a CHAIN.

CONNECTED IS NOT CLOSED.  A ring with one cell taken out is still one connected chain, so
this answers true on a wall you can walk straight through.  For an ENCLOSURE the verdict is
`flood_outside` + `leak_count`; this one is the contract for an open run.

api.sig: pub fn wall_offset_signed(w: Wall, px: float, py: float) -> float
api.doc:
── writing into the foxel — ALONG the wall, not ACROSS it (OD-12) ─────────

THE FIRST TRY MARKED THE WRONG EDGES.  The band model asked "does the wall's thin
rectangle overlap this hex edge?" — and the edges a thin band overlaps are the ones lying
ACROSS it, roughly perpendicular.  A due-east wall came out as a comb of vertical pickets
(`X28`), because a hex has edges on only three lines (30/90/150) and none runs east, so a
wall going east cannot BE a run of hex edges pointing east.

THE WALL IS A BOUNDARY, NOT A BAND.  A straight line divides the plane into two
half-planes.  The hex edges that lie ALONG the line are exactly the ones that SEPARATE a
cell on one side from a cell on the other — the boundary between the two half-planes, which
for any direction is a single connected chain, straight in the three edge directions and an
alternating wobble otherwise.  This is `housedraw::draw_walls`' own rule (an edge between an
inside cell and an outside one), applied to a half-plane instead of a filled region — so it
inherits `I3`'s "closed by construction, one wide" for free.

Signed perpendicular offset of a world point from the wall's centre line.  Positive on the
side the normal (-dy, dx) points to; the sign is all that matters for separation.

api.sig: pub fn wall_separates(w: Wall, cx: float, cy: float, nx: float, ny: float) -> boolean
pub fn hex_corner_x(q: integer, r: integer, c: integer) -> float
api.doc:
── THE EDGE TABLE IS hex_grid's, NOT OURS ─────────────────────────────────

`hex_grid` already owns the moros edge-wall model — it says so in the file: "walls live
on hex edges, stored on 3 canonical edges per hex (dirs 0,1,2); dirs 3,4,5 belong to the
neighbour".  So `hex_edge_corners(dir)` IS the map from a neighbour direction to the two
corners bounding that edge, and `moros_render::emit_hex_walls` emits exactly those corner
pairs (N = 5->0, NE = 0->1, SE = 1->2) for the three stored slots.

A PRIVATE CORNER CONVENTION IS A SILENT WRONG ANSWER.  This file first carried its own
table (corner 0 at 30 degrees) and paired edge `c` with `nb_q/nb_r(q, r, c)` — but
hex_field's direction order is [E, W, SE, SW, NE, NW] and hex_grid's is
[E, SE, SW, W, NW, NE], so five of the six edges were stored against the WRONG
neighbour.  Every gate stayed green: a consistently wrong edge is still written once,
still idempotent, still non-empty.  Only measuring the marks back against the geometry
caught it, which is why `wall_edge_gap` below is a gate and not a comment.

Corner `c` of the hex at (q,r), in world units — hex_grid's table, hex_grid's indices.

term for term — k*sqrt(3)/2 = sqrt(3)*(q + (r&1)/2) and m/2 = 1.5r — so this is the
integer spelling of `hex_to_px`, not a second convention.

pub fn wall_write(w: Wall, edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
THE ROUTINE: draw the wall into the foxel's three wall slots per hex.

An edge is marked iff the wall's centre line SEPARATES its two owning cells, within the run.
`edge_set_mat` stores an edge once, under whichever cell owns it, so writing from both sides
is idempotent — which is what makes the three-slots-per-hex model hold.

api.sig: pub fn wall_along_max(w: Wall, edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
── READING THE CHAIN BACK: is it ALONG the wall, and is it ONE chain? ─────

These are the two properties that distinguish the fixed marking from the old picket comb,
and neither is visible in the perpendicular STRAY (a comb and a zigzag both swing ~1 hex off
the line).  They are what `tests/wall.loft` §6 asserts.

ALONG-NESS.  For a marked edge between cells C and N, the vector C->N is PERPENDICULAR to the
edge.  An edge lying ALONG the wall therefore has C->N pointing ACROSS the wall — a small
`|C->N . wall_dir|`.  The old picket marked edges lying ACROSS the wall, whose C->N pointed
ALONG it — `|C->N . wall_dir| ~ 1`.

⚠ THAT MAKES THE WORST `|dot|` A DISCRIMINATOR ON HALF THE DIRECTIONS ONLY.  On the twelve
EXACT headings it tops out at 0.5 (N = 3) or 0.866 (N = 1), and nothing reaches 0.9.  On the
twelve IN-BETWEEN ones it reads **0.97** on completely correct output: a shallow line has to
cross the vertical edge between two cells of the SAME row wherever it steps up, and that
edge's dot is `cos(13.9 deg)`.  Measured, 3 of a 25-edge run are above 0.9.  So this number
describes the WOBBLE; it does not deliver a verdict, and a gate that thresholds it flags a
correct in-between wall.

The verdict is the CHAIN property below — two degree-1 vertices, no branches — which is exact
and holds for all 24 directions.

Example: @HXS-004

api.sig: pub fn wall_chain_ends(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
ONE CHAIN.  The marked edges form a connected path iff, keyed by their shared hex vertices
(exact triangle-lattice integers), exactly two vertices have degree 1 (the ends) and none has
degree > 2.  A picket comb of k disjoint edges has 2k degree-1 vertices — so this separates a
chain from a comb with no tolerance.  Returns the number of degree-1 vertices (2 for a single
chain, 0 for empty, 4 after a break, 2k for a comb).

⚠ TWO WALLS MEETING AT A CORNER USUALLY DO NOT FUSE, so this is 4 and not 2 for an L — each
wall keeps its own two ends.  That is a fact about the marking and not a defect: a consumer
reading it as *the marking is broken* will refuse a shape somebody drew on purpose.

Example: @HXS-004

api.sig: pub fn wall_chain_branches(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
Any vertex where three or more marked edges meet — a branch, which a straight wall's boundary
never has.  Non-zero means the marking is not a simple path.

Example: @HXS-004

api.sig: pub struct WallChain
api.doc:
── THE CHAIN IN READING ORDER ─────────────────────────────────────────────

The two counters above answer *how many ends* and *how many branches* and throw the walk
itself away, so a consumer holding a marking has the numbers and not the chain.  This
returns it: an unordered set of marked edges in, the vertices in the order a walk meets
them out — which is what `wall_read_run` and `surface_of` already consume, and what a scan
of the store can never give, because a scan has no order at all.

A CONSUMER WANTS THIS TO CUT A MARKING INTO RUNS.  `wall_read_run` reads a chain's two
ends and answers for one run; a marking with a CORNER in it has no such pair, and a closed
room has no free end at all.  With the chain ordered, the question becomes *where along it
does one run stop and the next begin*, which is a decision about spans rather than a search
over the plane.

⚠ ONE CALL IS ONE CHAIN, AND A MARKING IS OFTEN SEVERAL.  Two walls meeting at a corner do
not necessarily fuse — an L has FOUR degree-1 vertices, so each wall keeps its own two ends
and the marking is two chains.  `wc_n` is how many there are and `nth` picks one; a consumer
that walks one and stops describes half an L and calls the rest a residual.

⚠ A CLOSED LOOP HAS NO CANONICAL START.  With no degree-1 vertex the seed is the first
endpoint in scan order, which lands wherever the scan lands — so a room of four walls comes
back as one chain that begins and ends in the middle of the same wall.  `wc_loop` says so;
what to do about it belongs to the consumer, because only the consumer knows whether the
first and last spans it cut are one run.

⚠ AND AT A BRANCH THE ORDER IS ONE OF SEVERAL.  Where three or more marks meet, the walk
continues along the first unused one in scan order — deterministic, and *a* traversal rather
than *the* traversal.  `wc_branch` counts the vertices this chain passes through where that
choice was made, so a consumer needing a simple path can refuse rather than believe.

api.sig: pub fn wall_chain_walk(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer, wq: integer,
api.doc:
The `nth` chain of this marking, in the order a walk meets its vertices.  `nth = 0` is the
first; `wc_n` is how many there are, and is filled in whether or not `nth` names one.

api.sig: pub fn wall_offset_of(w: Wall, px: float, py: float) -> float
api.doc:
── EVALUATING THE MARKS BACK TO THE MESH (crawler / moros' own rule) ───────

This is the second half of the round trip, and it is NOT ours to invent: moros already
evaluates the three wall slots to geometry in `moros_render::emit_hex_walls`, and the
rule is one line — a marked edge becomes the quad standing on the segment between its
two corners.  `hex_edge_corners` is that segment, so the mesh a marked field produces is
fully determined here with no renderer, no `Mesh`, no graphics import.

WHAT THAT MESH IS.  It is the SAWTOOTH — the chain of hex edges the band crossed — not
the straight line we drew.  That is the honest state of the round trip: the foxel stores
where the wall went, and recovering the straight line from it is `rebuild`'s job.  So
the measurement below is not "does the mesh equal the wall" (it cannot) but "how far
does the mesh stray from it", which is the quantity the recovery has to undo.

Perpendicular distance from (px,py) to the wall's infinite centre line.

api.sig: pub fn wall_mesh_stray(w: Wall, edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
The worst perpendicular stray of any emitted segment endpoint, over the marked field.
Only edges whose midpoint lies within the run are measured — past the ends there is no
line to be near.

api.sig: pub fn wall_mesh_segments(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer,
api.doc:
How many distinct segments the mesh emitter would produce for the marked field — the
vertex count of moros' wall mesh divided by the per-edge quad, i.e. the segment count.

api.sig: pub fn wall_read_ends(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer, wq: integer, hq: integer)
api.doc:
The two degree-1 vertices of the marked chain, in triangle coordinates.  `ok` is false unless
there are exactly two — a fragmented or branching marking is REFUSED, never averaged into an
answer.

Example: @HXS-005

api.sig: pub fn wall_read_run(edges: EdgeSet, q0: integer, r0: integer, wq: integer, hq: integer)
api.doc:
Recover the whole run: direction, anchor and period count, all exact integers.  One period of
`d24` displaces a run by `3·tri(d24)`, so the endpoint displacement pins both `d24` and `p`; the
answer is canonicalised to the end that gives `p > 0`.  `ok` is false when the marking is not a
single chain, or when no direction divides the displacement — an unreadable field is REFUSED, not
approximated (law **P4**).

WHAT IT CANNOT RECOVER IS THE ORIENTATION, because the field does not store one: A-to-B and
B-to-A mark the identical edges.  The answer is canonicalised to `p > 0`, so the direction
comes back as `d24` OR as `d24 + 12` with the other endpoint as the anchor — both naming the
same wall.  `read.d == d` is therefore the wrong round-trip assertion; compare the ENDPOINTS.

api.doc:
The SOFFIT of a barrel vault or an arch: spring + sqrt(R^2 - d^2), d measured from the
crown line.  Beyond the springing the opening has closed, so the soffit is the springing
itself.  Pass a radius larger than the half-span for a segmental arch; equal to it for a
semicircular one.

api.sig: pub fn roof_hip(s: HexSet, f: Heights, eave: float, per_ring: float) -> integer
api.doc:
THE DISTANCE-TO-BOUNDARY ROOF — the one that actually matters on a quantised footprint.

Every cell rises at a constant slope from its NEAREST EAVE, which is the definition of a
hip roof. On a circular footprint that is a cone; on an octagonal one a pyramid; on an
L-shaped hall a properly mitred hip-and-valley. The FORM is entirely the footprint's
shape — there is one function here, not a catalogue, and that is the whole reason "roof
forms" stopped being a list.

Driving it from the FOOTPRINT rather than from the ideal circle is also what makes the
eave level. Boundary cells are at ring 0 by definition, whatever their true radius. Drive
a cone from each cell's own radius instead and the eave inherits the footprint's
roundness deviation, wobbling by slope x that spread — rooftest measures both, because
the failure is invisible until you look at the eave rather than the apex.

Multi-source BFS inward from the boundary, on the pre-allocated array + index-write
idiom (appending while a head pointer walks the same vector is the broken shape).

api.sig: pub fn dome(s: HexSet, f: Heights, cx: float, cy: float, base: float, radius: float)
api.doc:
A DOME — a point source with a CIRCULAR profile, where a cone is a point source with a
linear one.  That single swap is the whole difference, and it is also why a dome is the
harder object: a cone's slope is constant, a dome's diverges at the springing
(dz/dr = -r/sqrt(R^2-r^2)).  Past the 45-degree point r = R/sqrt(2) the surface is more
wall than roof and a per-cell height stops being able to carry it — which is exactly why
real domes sit on a vertical DRUM and only the cap is vaulted.  vaulttest measures it.

Example: @HXR-006
⛔ **AND WHEN NOTHING FITS, IT SAYS SO — `ROOF_UNKNOWN`.**  This returned the least-bad of
the three with `rf_kind` naming a shape the field is NOT, and the residual was the only
signal that it was a fallback rather than a recovery.  Measured on fields THIS PACKAGE
DRAWS: a `roof_ridge` gable comes back `ROOF_CONE` at residual **1.209**, with an apex of
6.318 where the truth is 6.0 and a slope of 0.409 where it is 0.5; a `roof_hip` comes back
`ROOF_CONE` at **0.615**.  `roof_eval` then evaluates that cone into a surface that is not
the roof.

⚠ **THE BEST CANDIDATE'S PARAMETERS ARE KEPT**, because *which* shape came closest and by
how much is what a caller diagnoses with.  What changes is that `rf_kind` no longer CLAIMS
one — `roof_eval` draws nothing for `ROOF_UNKNOWN` — so a fallback can no longer be
mistaken for a recovery by a caller that reads the kind and trusts it.

⚠ **NO EXISTING RECOVERY CHANGES.**  A candidate within `tol` returns exactly as before;
only the path where all three were already wrong is affected, which is precisely the
population that was being told the wrong thing.

⚠ **AND THE MISSING KIND IS NAMED RATHER THAN GUESSED AT**: this package DRAWS a ridge, a
hip and three vaults, and fits a plane, a cone and a dome.  A ridge is the cone's own
profile about a SEGMENT instead of a point, so `roof_ridge_fit` is a well-specified
addition — until it exists, a gable is honestly unknown rather than dishonestly a cone.

api.sig: pub fn roof_ridge_fit(s: HexSet, f: Heights) -> RoofFit
api.doc:
⛔ **FOUR SEEDS, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS ANY GOOD — THE OTHERS ARE KEPT AS CHEAP INSURANCE.**  0.1.2
started both ends at `roof_cone_fit`'s centre, reasoning that a cone is a ridge whose segment
has zero length.  It is — but the cone fit RUNS AWAY on ridge-like data: fitting a cone to a
gable puts its apex far outside the footprint (the same degeneracy that sends it to x = 9744
on a plane), and a local search started there never walks back.  Measured on a real roof — a
27-cell gable, constant across the ridge — it returned a DEGENERATE segment 8 world units
clear of the roof with slope 0 and residual 1.185.

✅ **So the climb is run from all three and the best is kept**: both ends at the highest cell,
both at the cone's centre, and one at each.  Each is cheap, and *take the better of two
starts* is not a threshold — it is the same answer either way when both converge.

⚠ **A LOCAL SEARCH THAT HAS TO GROW A SEGMENT OUT OF A POINT IS THE FRAGILE PART**, not the
seed: from a degenerate start the residual can be flat in every direction the first step
tries.  Two starts that fail differently are what makes that visible.

⚠ **THE LIBRARY'S OWN FIXTURE DID NOT CATCH THIS** — a ridge drawn on a disc happened to give
a usable cone centre.  The consumer's roof did.  That is `probe/adopt`'s lesson in a library:
a suite written by the author cannot ask the questions the author does not have.

⚠ **EACH END IS CLIMBED IN THE EIGHT DIRECTIONS `roof_cone_fit` USES, ON THE SAME STEP
SCHEDULE.**  A second search rule here would be a second opinion about how this family
searches.

hip roof. On a circular footprint that is a cone; on an octagonal one a pyramid; on an
L-shaped hall a properly mitred hip-and-valley. The FORM is entirely the footprint's
shape — there is one function here, not a catalogue, and that is the whole reason "roof
forms" stopped being a list.

Driving it from the FOOTPRINT rather than from the ideal circle is also what makes the
eave level. Boundary cells are at ring 0 by definition, whatever their true radius. Drive
a cone from each cell's own radius instead and the eave inherits the footprint's
roundness deviation, wobbling by slope x that spread — rooftest measures both, because
the failure is invisible until you look at the eave rather than the apex.

Multi-source BFS inward from the boundary, on the pre-allocated array + index-write
idiom (appending while a head pointer walks the same vector is the broken shape).

Example: @HXR-002

api.sig: pub fn dome(s: HexSet, f: Heights, cx: float, cy: float, base: float, radius: float)
api.doc:
A DOME — a point source with a CIRCULAR profile, where a cone is a point source with a
linear one.  That single swap is the whole difference, and it is also why a dome is the
harder object: a cone's slope is constant, a dome's diverges at the springing
(dz/dr = -r/sqrt(R^2-r^2)).  Past the 45-degree point r = R/sqrt(2) the surface is more
wall than roof and a per-cell height stops being able to carry it — which is exactly why
real domes sit on a vertical DRUM and only the cap is vaulted.  vaulttest measures it.

api.doc: Example: @HXR-004

api.sig: pub fn vault_cloister(s: HexSet, f: Heights, t1: Track, t2: Track,
api.doc: Example: @HXR-004

api.doc: What can pass here: the gap between floor and soffit.

api.sig: pub fn roof_ponds(s: HexSet, f: Heights) -> integer
api.doc:
PONDING — the roof's correctness invariant, and the analogue of a stair's monotonicity.
An INTERIOR cell (all six neighbours in the footprint) every one of whose neighbours is
strictly higher is a local minimum: water collects and never leaves. A roof that sheds
has none. Boundary cells are exempt — they drain off the eave, which is their job.

A zero here is not "no local minima": a hollow on the BOUNDARY is not counted.

api.doc:
The spread of eave heights around a footprint's boundary — 0 for a level eave.

THE INSTRUMENT FOR THE FAILURE NOTHING ELSE SEES: a roof built from the wrong distance
source still has an apex, still is not flat and still sheds water.  This is the number
that moves.

api.sig: pub struct RoofFit
pub fn roof_plane_fit(s: HexSet, f: Heights) -> RoofFit
api.doc: Least squares z = a*x + b*y + c.  Covers flat and every shed/mono-pitch.

api.sig: pub fn roof_ridge_fit(s: HexSet, f: Heights) -> RoofFit
api.doc:
⛔ **FOUR SEEDS, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS ANY GOOD — THE OTHERS ARE KEPT AS CHEAP INSURANCE.**  0.1.2
started both ends at `roof_cone_fit`'s centre, reasoning that a cone is a ridge whose segment
has zero length.  It is — but the cone fit RUNS AWAY on ridge-like data: fitting a cone to a
gable puts its apex far outside the footprint (the same degeneracy that sends it to x = 9744
on a plane), and a local search started there never walks back.  Measured on a real roof — a
27-cell gable, constant across the ridge — it returned a DEGENERATE segment 8 world units
clear of the roof with slope 0 and residual 1.185.

✅ **So the climb is run from all three and the best is kept**: both ends at the highest cell,
both at the cone's centre, and one at each.  Each is cheap, and *take the better of two
starts* is not a threshold — it is the same answer either way when both converge.

⚠ **A LOCAL SEARCH THAT HAS TO GROW A SEGMENT OUT OF A POINT IS THE FRAGILE PART**, not the
seed: from a degenerate start the residual can be flat in every direction the first step
tries.  Two starts that fail differently are what makes that visible.

⚠ **THE LIBRARY'S OWN FIXTURE DID NOT CATCH THIS** — a ridge drawn on a disc happened to give
a usable cone centre.  The consumer's roof did.  That is `probe/adopt`'s lesson in a library:
a suite written by the author cannot ask the questions the author does not have.

⚠ **EACH END IS CLIMBED IN THE EIGHT DIRECTIONS `roof_cone_fit` USES, ON THE SAME STEP
SCHEDULE.**  A second search rule here would be a second opinion about how this family
searches.

api.sig: pub fn roof_cone_fit(s: HexSet, f: Heights) -> RoofFit
pub fn roof_dome_fit(s: HexSet, f: Heights) -> RoofFit
pub fn roof_match(s: HexSet, f: Heights, tol: float) -> RoofFit
api.doc:
Decide what the field IS.  A plane wins ties: it is the simpler statement, and a cone
fitted to a flat roof would put its apex somewhere arbitrary.

Example: @HXR-006
⛔ **AND WHEN NOTHING FITS, IT SAYS SO — `ROOF_UNKNOWN`.**  This returned the least-bad of
the three with `rf_kind` naming a shape the field is NOT, and the residual was the only
signal that it was a fallback rather than a recovery.  Measured on fields THIS PACKAGE
DRAWS: a `roof_ridge` gable comes back `ROOF_CONE` at residual **1.209**, with an apex of
6.318 where the truth is 6.0 and a slope of 0.409 where it is 0.5; a `roof_hip` comes back
`ROOF_CONE` at **0.615**.  `roof_eval` then evaluates that cone into a surface that is not
the roof.

⚠ **THE BEST CANDIDATE'S PARAMETERS ARE KEPT**, because *which* shape came closest and by
how much is what a caller diagnoses with.  What changes is that `rf_kind` no longer CLAIMS
one — `roof_eval` draws nothing for `ROOF_UNKNOWN` — so a fallback can no longer be
mistaken for a recovery by a caller that reads the kind and trusts it.

⚠ **NO EXISTING RECOVERY CHANGES.**  A candidate within `tol` returns exactly as before;
only the path where all three were already wrong is affected, which is precisely the
population that was being told the wrong thing.

⚠ **AND THE MISSING KIND IS NAMED RATHER THAN GUESSED AT**: this package DRAWS a ridge, a
hip and three vaults, and fits a plane, a cone and a dome.  A ridge is the cone's own
profile about a SEGMENT instead of a point, so `roof_ridge_fit` is a well-specified
addition — until it exists, a gable is honestly unknown rather than dishonestly a cone.

api.sig: pub fn roof_eval(fit: RoofFit, x: float, y: float) -> float
api.doc:
The recovered ANALYTIC surface — what a renderer should draw, at any resolution, instead
of the cells it came from.

api.sig: pub struct Draft
pub fn draft_new(f: Form, d: integer, a: integer, b: integer, p: integer) -> Draft
pub fn draft_has_run(s: Draft) -> boolean
pub fn draft_write(s: Draft, name: text) -> text
api.doc:
The text of a stencil: the form's spelling, then — if there is one — a single `wall` line.
One line, one record, same shape as `side`: the reader refuses anything else rather than
repairing it (`X39`).

⚠ THIS IS NOT THE CANONICAL TEXT.  It writes the spelling it is GIVEN, and both the form's
start corner and the run's direction are choices the model does not fix — so two calls can
spell one stencil two ways.  A round trip diffs against `draft_canon_text`.

Example: @HXI-001

api.sig: pub fn draft_read(t: text) -> Draft
api.doc:
Parse.  The `side` lines go to `form_read` unchanged; a trailing `wall` line is this layer's.
A malformed record yields a stencil with an empty form — REFUSED, never repaired.

THAT WAS A CLAIM BEFORE IT WAS A TEST, and it was wrong the same way `hex_form`'s reader was
(that one was measured first; this line inherited both the `word_int(…) ?? 0` helper and the
gap).  A nineteen-cell acceptance matrix admitted ten texts `draft_write` cannot emit and
re-wrote each of them differently: a trailing space, an extra field, `+3`, `003`, a `wall`
line placed between two `side` lines — and, sharper than any spelling, a field that is not a
number at all.  `wall d x a -6 b 9 p 1` became `d 0`: not a wall that is missing, A WALL
POINTING SOMEWHERE ELSE, admitted into the model without a word.  `a x` moved it instead.

What pins it now is the same RE-SPELLING IDENTITY: a field is an integer only if printing the
parse reproduces the original characters, a line is a record only if it carries exactly the
fields the writer emits, and the `wall` line is LAST because that is where the writer puts it.

Example: @HXI-003

api.sig: pub fn draft_draw(s: Draft, cq: integer, cr: integer, cells: HexSet, edges: EdgeSet,
api.doc:
Draw the whole stencil into one field: the fill, its own boundary walls, and the embedded run as
material on INTERIOR edges only.  Returns the number of interior edges the run marked.

api.sig: pub fn draft_interior(cells: HexSet, edges: EdgeSet, embedmat: integer) -> EdgeSet
api.doc:
The INTERIOR edges carrying `embedmat`, isolated — what the run reader consumes.  Boundary edges
(one cell out) are the stencil's own walls and are never part of a run.

api.sig: pub fn draft_rebuild_text(cells: HexSet, edges: EdgeSet, name: text, embedmat: integer) -> text
api.doc:
REBUILD, INCLUDING THE RUN.  The form comes from the cells (constructive recovery, `X45`); the
run comes from the interior edges (`wall_read_run`, `X60`) — two recoveries reading disjoint
slots.  An unreadable run is REFUSED, so it is dropped loudly by a text diff rather than silently.

⚠ DIFF THIS AGAINST `draft_canon_text`, NOT against `draft_write`.  What comes back is the
spelling the FIELD answers with, and for the run half that is one of two — see the note there.

Example: @HXI-002

api.sig: pub fn draft_canon(s: Draft, cells: HexSet) -> Draft
api.doc:
── ONE MODEL, ONE TEXT — the canonical spelling ───────────────────────────

The format's premise is that a `diff` means *the model changed*, which needs every model to
have exactly ONE text.  The form half has that: a shape has n cyclic spellings and `form_canon`
picks the smallest, which is why `rebuild_construct_text` and `form_canon_text` agree.

THE RUN HALF HAD NO SUCH RULE, and a run has exactly TWO spellings — `(d, A, p)` and
`(d + 12, B, p)` — because A-to-B and B-to-A mark the identical edges and the field stores no
orientation (`wall_read_run`'s own note).  Measured over all 24 directions: the two spellings
draw fields that differ in ZERO edges, and **exactly one of them survives a text round trip**,
never both and never neither.  So an author who wrote the wall from the other end got *the
model changed* out of a byte diff on a model that had not changed at all.

The canonical spelling is therefore READ OFF THE FIELD rather than chosen by a rule — the same
discipline `hexfit`'s feature grid is built on (`SPEC` **L11**: consult the table that owns the
answer), and the only definition that cannot drift from what `draft_rebuild_text` will answer,
since it is that same reader.

Example: @HXI-001

api.sig: pub fn draft_canon_text(s: Draft, cells: HexSet, name: text) -> text
api.doc:
The one text a round trip can be diffed against.  A run that does not FIT is left as written —
the canon is a spelling rule, not a doorstep, and refusing here would hide which of the two is
wrong.

Example: @HXI-001

pub fn draft_fits(s: Draft, cells: HexSet) -> integer

specific restriction, never a bare false.

api.sig: pub fn arc_is_shell(n24: integer) -> boolean
pub fn arc_fits(n24: integer) -> integer
pub fn arc_fit_n(n24: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
The nearest realisable shell — `K-FIT` says *nearest*, so this can offer a LARGER disk than the
author asked for (N = 11 is offered 12, not 0).  That is deliberate and differs from what the
unrefused value would have drawn: an off-grid N silently draws the shell BELOW it, so `arc_fill`
would have given 0.  Offering the nearest and showing the residual is the point — the author sees
both candidates' cost — `arc_snap_n` is the other one — instead of being quietly rounded down.
Ties go DOWN, to the smaller shell.

Example: @HXI-006

api.sig: pub fn arc_fit_residual(n24: integer) -> integer
pub fn arc_snap_n(n24: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
THE OTHER CANDIDATE, and the reason the comment above can say *both*.  This is the shell an
UNREFUSED radius actually draws — the largest realisable one at or below `n24` — so an editor
can show the author what the silent snap would have cost beside what the offer costs.  The two
are not close: `N = 35` is offered 36 at a residual of 1 and would have drawn **12**, an error
of 23 in the same units, because 12 and 36 are neighbouring shells.  Verified against
`arc_fill` over every radius 0..64 rather than against the formula it shares with `arc_fits`.

Example: @HXI-006

api.sig: pub fn arc_snap_residual(n24: integer) -> integer
pub fn level_fits(lv: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
── LEVELS — MEASURED TO HAVE NOTHING TO REFUSE ─────────────────────────────

A level is the topological SHEET (`X58`), stored as an integer (`ha_cy` / `ck_cy`) and used as a
FILTER BEFORE THE CUT.  There is no continuous parameter here, so `I-QUANT` has nothing to say:
nothing exists *between* two levels to be snapped to one of them.  Measured over the full range
an integer holds — the behaviour at ±10^6 is identical to the behaviour at 0.

This returns `FIT_OK` unconditionally, and that is a RESULT, not an omission.  `tests/fit.loft`
keeps it honest the only way an always-true predicate can be kept honest: by showing that the
SAME doorstep refuses the other parameters, so "accepts every level" is not "accepts everything".

Example: @HXI-008

api.sig: pub fn mat_fits(m: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
⚠ NO OFFER, AND THAT IS THE POINT.  `K-FIT` says a refusal offers *the nearest fitting
alternative* — which presumes an ORDINAL parameter, where "nearest" means "almost what you
asked for".  A material id is NOMINAL: it is a name, not a magnitude.  The nearest admissible id
to 256 is 255, and 255 is a *different material* — offering it would be worse than a blank no,
because it looks like a small correction and is not.  So this refusal names its restriction and
stops there.  The author must pick a material, not accept a rounding.
