rate it could not state in the first place.  Same distinction
`tick_bank.loft` § THE RATE IS SCALED AND THE TIME IS NOT draws one
family over — except that a clock's rate is authored by a KEYPRESS
rather than by `numbers.json`, so it is exact rather than quantised.

⚠ **Pause is `0 / 1`**, and it banks nothing while keeping what is
banked — so unpausing resumes mid-step rather than re-phasing the
simulation.  A step of 0 is a mistake, never a pause
(`clock_new`).

⚠ A negative `num` is clamped to 0 rather than rewinding.  Time
going backwards is dropped everywhere else in this file, and a rate
that ran the simulation in reverse would need every consumer to have
an inverse tick.

⚠ **Changing the rate DROPS the wall carry**, because the carry is
measured in `den`-ths of a base unit and the old `den` is gone.  It
is under one base unit — a third of a microsecond — and a rate
change is an event a player caused, not a per-frame path.
Example: @FIX-007

api.sig: pub fn clock_rate_num(clk: const TickClock) -> integer
api.doc: The rate's numerator — 0 for a paused clock.

api.sig: pub fn clock_rate_den(clk: const TickClock) -> integer
api.doc: The rate's denominator — never 0, and 1 for an unconfigured clock.

api.sig: pub fn clock_advance(clk: TickClock, elapsed: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Spend elapsed time, and answer the whole steps it bought.

⚠ **Integer division, not a subtraction loop.**  The loop is what
lost the tick — eleven subtractions of a repeating fraction leave a
remainder a hair under the twelfth — and it is also O(steps), so a
frame that delivered an hour walked five thousand iterations to say
so.  One division answers both.

⚠ **Time going backwards is DROPPED, not banked.**  A negative
elapsed is a clock that was reset or a caller subtracting in the
wrong order; banking it would owe the simulation negative ticks and
then swallow the next real frame.  Answering 0 and keeping the bank
is the only behaviour that cannot corrupt a run.

⚠ **No cap, and `clock_advance_capped` is the door that has one.**
A frame that delivers 20 s buys 30 ticks here, which is the property
dryopea's 654 gate measurements rest on.
Example: @FIX-001

api.sig: pub fn clock_advance_capped(clk: TickClock, elapsed: integer,
api.doc:
The same, for a driver that may have been backgrounded — at most
`max_steps`, and the excess is GONE.

⚠⚠ **It DROPS rather than defers, and the difference is the whole
door.**  `clock_advance` has already reduced the bank to the
sub-step remainder by the time this clamps, so the steps beyond the
cap are not owed: the next frame answers 1, not a burst.  The
tempting wrong version clamps the answer and leaves the backlog
banked, which runs the simulation behind the wall for ever after —
`tests/26_l4` § A cap that defers is that version, kept as the
control, and it is the only thing that makes this function's gate
non-trivial.

⚠ **And it must not compress**, which is moros's own note: *a
compressed catch-up is the variable-step bug wearing a bound's
clothes*.  Nothing here can — the step is fixed and this answers a
COUNT — but a driver that multiplied its tick's dt to "catch up"
would reintroduce exactly what `plans/22` § LOD is warned against.

⚠ A cap below 1 is clamped to 1, for `clock_new`'s reason: a cap of
zero is a simulation that can never advance, which is a mistake
rather than a mode.  Pause is a rate of 0.
Example: @FIX-004

api.sig: pub fn clock_pump(clk: TickClock, now: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Spend the time since the last reading of an ABSOLUTE wall clock.

⚠ **The server pump's door: it owns the wall and the caller owns no
subtraction.**  `now - last` written at the call site is where a
driver gets the order backwards once and silently swallows a frame —
`clock_advance` drops negative time, so the mistake looks like a
stutter rather than an error.

⚠ **The FIRST call primes and answers none.**  A pump whose first
reading was treated as elapsed would open a server with its whole
uptime as one burst of ticks.

⚠ **A wall going backwards re-primes** rather than dropping the
reading, because an absolute clock that jumped back is the new truth;
dropping it would owe every future pump the difference.

⚠ No cap — moros's server has none and `plans/26` § 3 says why the
two repos are both right.  A pump that needs one wraps this in the
same clamp `clock_advance_capped` applies.
Example: @FIX-003

api.sig: pub fn clock_step(clk: const TickClock, n: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Ask for `n` steps, and answer how many that was.

⚠ **It does not touch the bank, and that is the whole point of it
being a separate door.**  A count is not elapsed time: a script
saying `tick 30` neither spends a live session's remainder nor
leaves one behind.  `play.loft` § TWO ways to ask made this
distinction one level up and measured what folding them costs.

⚠ It looks trivial and is not free to delete: without it a caller
that has a count must spell it as `n * step`, which is the exact
mistake `tests/19_p1` records — and which is only safe here because
the arithmetic is integer.  The door is what says so.
Example: @FIX-002

api.sig: pub fn clock_step_units(clk: const TickClock) -> integer
api.doc: The step this clock ticks on, in base units.

api.sig: pub fn clock_banked(clk: const TickClock) -> integer
api.doc:
Time banked toward the next step, in base units — always in
`[0, step)`.

⚠ **Readable so a run can be RESTORED**, which is the whole of what
a rollback consumer needs from the timing half (`plans/26` § What
this plan does NOT build): re-running N steps from a restored bank
is bit-identical because `clock_step` is exact.
Example: @FIX-006

api.sig: pub fn clock_restore(clk: TickClock, banked: integer)
api.doc:
Put a clock back where it was — the other half of `clock_banked`.

⚠ Clamped into `[0, step)` rather than trusted: a bank at or past
the step is a state `clock_advance` can never leave behind, and
accepting one would make the next call answer a step nobody's time
paid for.

api.sig: pub fn clock_alpha(clk: const TickClock) -> float
api.doc:
How far the bank is toward the next step, in `[0, 1)`.

⚠ **The one number a renderer needs from a fixed-step clock**, and
the reason it is here rather than at the call site: `banked / step`
written by hand is a caller reaching INTO the accumulator, and a
caller that can read `banked` can also write it.  This is the read
door, and `clock_banked` (raw units, for save/restore) is the other
one — two questions, two answers, one field.

⚠ **Half-open by construction, not by a clamp.**  `clock_advance`
leaves `banked` in `[0, step)` and `clock_restore` refuses anything
else, so the division cannot reach 1.0 — which is what a caller
lerping between two states depends on: an alpha of exactly 1.0 would
draw the NEXT state one frame early, on the frame before the tick
that produces it.

⚠⚠ **What a consumer does with it is a PRESENTATION decision and this
file must not make it.**  The textbook use is
`lerp(previous_state, current_state, alpha)` — and dryopea measured it
against two alternatives over one drive (`tests/26_l5_the_alpha.loft`,
`@M035`):

* `lerp(prev, cur, alpha)` draws the step that has ALREADY happened,
so it is **exactly one step behind, for ever** — 2.598 m here,
because a step is 2/3 of a second;
* `cur + alpha·(cur − prev)` is **exact to machine precision** while
the velocity holds, and jumps a whole step's travel on the frame
the mover starts or stops;
* a first-order ease toward `cur` needs no previous state, lags
between the two, and is the only one whose picture depends on the
frames it was drawn on.

⚠ Three prices on three different axes, and which one is right is a
function of how long the STEP is — so a clock that picked one would be
wrong for every consumer whose step is a different length.  This
answers *where between two steps are we*; it does not answer *what
should be drawn there*.
Example: @FIX-005

api.sig: pub fn clock_drive(slow: TickClock, fast: const TickClock, n: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Spend `n` steps of `fast` on `slow`, and answer the slow steps that
bought.

⚠⚠ **The case is a strategy layer over a unit layer** — dryopea has
the shape twice already (the camera steps at frame rate while the sim
steps at 1.5 Hz, and `plans/22` § LOD contemplates ticking distant
things every N ticks).  ⚠ **And it is the OPPOSITE of that plan's
warning**: *bank progress, never multiply it* refuses to give a
distant enemy `N × dt` of movement in one tick.  This gives a slower
CLOCK the time those N ticks took, and it still ticks one step at a
time.

⚠ **Spelling it `n * step` at the call site is the shape of mistake
`tests/19_p1` records** — a count folded into a duration, wrong for
602 of the first 1000 `n`.  Here it is exact, because both sides are
integers; the door exists so that the next consumer does not
re-derive it in seconds and find out the hard way, and
`tests/26_l4` § Composing by hand is exact says so out loud rather
than letting this comment overclaim.

⚠ **A slow clock driven this way LAGS its driver by less than one
fast step, and never leads.**  The fast clock's own bank is time
that has not become a tick yet, so it has not been handed on — which
is the correct answer and not an approximation: the composed clock is
exactly as far along as the ticks that actually happened.

⚠ **`slow`'s own rate still applies.**  A rate set on both clocks
multiplies, which is a composition a caller asked for; set it on the
one that faces the wall.
Example: @FIX-008

api.sig: pub struct Timer
api.doc:
A one-shot duration and how much of it has been spent.

⚠ **Both integers, and `total == 0` is UNARMED** — the zero-default
that makes a partial struct literal correct everywhere this replaces
a `0.0` seconds field.  See the header.

api.sig: pub fn timer_new() -> Timer
api.doc: A timer nobody has armed.

api.sig: pub fn timer_armed(units: integer) -> Timer
api.doc:
A timer armed for `units` — the factory, for a struct literal that
wants one already running.

⚠ `Enemy`'s pre-walk window is the case: an enemy is built already
standing, so the field has to arrive armed.

api.sig: pub fn timer_arm(t: Timer, units: integer)
api.doc:
Arm it for `units`, from zero.

⚠ **A duration of zero or less DISARMS rather than firing.**  Both
readings are defensible and this one is what the call sites already
mean: a schedule authored with a lull of 0 sends the next wave
immediately because nothing is running, not because a timer fired.
⚠ It also re-arms from wherever it was, so a boost pressed during a
boost restarts the clock rather than extending it — the behaviour the
float version had, stated rather than inherited.
Example: @FIX-011

api.sig: pub fn timer_running(t: const Timer) -> boolean
api.doc: Is this timer running — armed, and not yet fired?

api.sig: pub fn timer_left(t: const Timer) -> integer
api.doc:
Base units still to go.  Zero for a timer that is not running.

⚠ **The DOWN reading**, and it is a subtraction rather than a second
field.  `helper.recover` and `Vehicle.boost_left` were both stored
this way and each carried its own epsilon; there is one number now
and it is exact.

api.sig: pub fn timer_spent(t: const Timer) -> integer
api.doc:
Base units gone by.  Zero for a timer that is not running.

⚠ **The UP reading**, off the same number.  `TowerCharge.repair` was
stored this way — *seconds banked toward the rebuild* — because zero
had to mean "nobody is working on it", and that is still what an
unarmed timer says.

api.sig: pub fn timer_total(t: const Timer) -> integer
api.doc: The whole duration this timer was armed for, in base units.

api.sig: pub fn timer_fraction(t: const Timer) -> float
api.doc:
How far through it is, in `[0, 1)` — 0.0 for a timer that is not
running.

⚠ **The presentation door, and the one place a float appears** — a
HUD showing a rebuild part-done, exactly `bank_fraction`'s position
one family over.  Nothing in the simulation may read it: a
comparison against 1.0 here is the epsilon problem walking back in
through the display.

api.sig: pub fn timer_spend(t: Timer, units: integer) -> boolean
api.doc:
Spend `units` of it.  Answers whether THIS call finished it.

⚠ **It fires exactly once and then disarms**, which is the whole
difference from `bank_gain`: the remainder past the boundary is
DISCARDED, because a one-shot's residue means nothing afterwards.
Carrying it would make the next arming shorter than the one before —
measured in `tests/26_l3` § A one-shot built on a bank, where a 5.0 s
cooldown costs 8 ticks the first time and 7 the second.

⚠ A timer that is not running answers false and stays that way, so a
caller may spend into it unconditionally — which is what
`vehicle_burn` does with the cooldown every single tick.

⚠ Non-positive time is dropped rather than owed, for
`clock_advance`'s reason: time going backwards must not un-fire
anything.
Example: @FIX-011

api.sig: pub fn timer_cancel(t: Timer)
api.doc:
Stop it without firing.

⚠ **A door of its own rather than `timer_arm(t, 0)`, because it is a
DECISION** — the same argument `bank_reset` makes.  A vehicle that
respawns loses the boost it was in the middle of; a cooldown that is
merely running keeps everything.  Two behaviours, and the one that
throws work away says so by name.

api.sig: pub fn timer_restore_left(t: Timer, left: integer, total: integer)
api.doc:
Put a timer back from a DOWN reading — `units` left of `total`.

⚠ Clamped rather than trusted, for `clock_restore`'s reason: `left`
past `total` is a state `timer_spend` can never leave behind, and a
`left` of zero or less is a timer that has already fired, which is an
unarmed one.

api.sig: pub fn timer_restore_spent(t: Timer, spent: integer, total: integer)
api.doc:
Put a timer back from an UP reading — `units` spent of `total`.

⚠ The other half, and the two are not interchangeable at the call
site: `emit.loft` writes whichever reading its field was authored in,
so a tower's rebuild round-trips as *banked* and a helper's recovery
as *left*.

api.sig: pub fn ease_fraction(k: float, dt: float) -> float
api.doc:
What one frame of `dt` closes of a gap, in `[0, 1)`.

⚠ Zero for a frame with no time in it — which is what a PAUSED
consumer hands down, and it must not creep.

Example: @FIX-012

api.sig: pub fn approach(now: float, want: float, k: float, dt: float) -> float
api.doc:
Move `now` toward `want` by one frame's worth.

⚠ **`k` is the gap fraction closed per SECOND**, so it is a rate and
not a step: an approach chasing something moving at `v` settles at a
steady lag of `v / k`.  ⚠⚠ That derivation assumes a CONTINUOUS
target — against one that stands still and then jumps a whole step,
the real excursion is the step, not `v / k`, and a consumer that
sized `k` on the formula will be out by the ratio of the two
(measured at **3.7x** in this package's first consumer).

Example: @FIX-012

api.sig: pub fn wrap_deg(a: float) -> float
api.doc: An angle in degrees, folded into `[0, 360)`.

api.sig: pub fn wrap_delta(d: float) -> float
api.doc:
A DIFFERENCE of angles, folded into `(−180, 180]` — the short way
round.

⚠⚠ **This is not defensive tidying, and a real key set reaches the
wrong-way swing.**  In this package's first consumer, holding one key
gives a bearing of 360° and adding a second gives 60°.  The true turn
is 60°; eased as plain numbers it is **−300°**, and the camera spins
five sixths of a circle the wrong way on one extra keypress — while
looking like a working camera the whole time, which is why it needs a
test rather than an eye.

Example: @FIX-013

api.sig: pub fn approach_angle(now: float, want: float, k: float, dt: float) -> float
api.doc:
Move an ANGLE toward another by one frame's worth, the short way.

⚠ A separate door from `approach` rather than a flag on it: an angle
is not a number that happens to wrap, and a consumer that eased a
bearing with `approach` gets a camera that is correct at every angle
except across the seam.

Example: @FIX-013

api.sig: pub struct Bank
api.doc:
Progress banked toward the next whole unit.

⚠ **One field, and the struct exists so the caller cannot forget to
write the remainder back.**  loft has no by-reference integer, so a
free function over an `integer` would have to answer a pair and
leave the carry to the call site — which is the seven-sites problem
wearing a library's clothes.  Passed as a parameter it aliases, so
`bank_gain` updates it in place and answers only the whole units.

api.sig: pub fn bank_new() -> Bank
api.doc: A bank with nothing carried.

api.sig: pub fn bank_whole(units_per_second: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
How much banked progress makes one whole unit, for a clock counting
`units_per_second` base units a second.

⚠ dryopea's answer is the `BANK_WHOLE` constant above; this is the
derivation, for a consumer whose clock counts something else.

api.sig: pub fn bank_rate(per_second: float) -> integer
api.doc:
Quantise a rate quoted in whole units per second.

⚠ **It ROUNDS rather than truncating**, and the difference is
visible at every rate that is not a whole millionth: truncating
would make a mover systematically slower, which is the shape of
defect this whole plan exists to remove.  ⚠ Truncation is also what
`@D003` was — the same mistake one unit further out.

api.sig: pub fn bank_gain(b: Bank, rate: integer, elapsed: integer,
api.doc:
Gain ground at `rate` for `elapsed` base time units, and answer the
whole units it releases.  The remainder stays banked.

⚠ **This is the one implementation of *do not lose a fraction* in
dryopea**, and it is exact: `progress` is an integer, `rate ×
elapsed` is an integer, and a whole unit costs an integer, so there
is nothing to round and no epsilon to get the direction of wrong
(`CLAUDE.md` § Timers and epsilons: *neither direction is safe*).

⚠ **A rate of zero banks nothing and keeps what is banked** — a
mover that stops has not forgotten how far it had come.  Same for a
non-positive `elapsed`: `tick_clock.loft` gives the reason time
going backwards must be dropped rather than owed.

⚠ **What it does NOT do is decide whether the mover may move.**
`enemy_tick` asks the pre-walk window first, `helper_tick` asks
whether the crew member is alive; a bank that knew about standing
would have to know about every other reason not to move too.
Example: @FIX-009

api.sig: pub fn bank_most(rate: integer, elapsed: integer, whole: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
The MOST one step at `rate` over `elapsed` could release — the
ceiling, carry included, touching no bank.

⚠ **An upper bound is a different question from a release**, and
conflating them is what a caller does when it has no bank to spend.
`play.loft::play_steer_reach` is the case: it asks how far ahead a
held key should point, which must exceed anything one tick can
cover, and it must not consume the player's carry to find out.
Example: @FIX-010

api.sig: pub fn bank_progress(b: const Bank) -> integer
api.doc:
What is banked, in raw progress.

⚠ **Readable so a run can be COMPARED and RESTORED** —
`compare.loft::state_diff` reads it as part of a mover's state, and
it is an integer now, so the comparison is exact without the
"floats EXACTLY" argument that file had to make.

api.sig: pub fn bank_fraction(b: const Bank, whole: integer) -> float
api.doc:
What is banked, as a fraction of a whole unit.

⚠ **The AUTHORING door, and the one place a float appears** —
`emit.loft` writes a captured situation as `.keys` text and
`script.loft` reads it back, and *hexes* is the unit a person
authors in.  The round trip is exact because a double carries 53
bits and `BANK_WHOLE` needs 42: `bank_restore_fraction` recovers the
integer this answered.

api.sig: pub fn bank_restore(b: Bank, progress: integer, whole: integer)
api.doc:
Put a bank back where it was, in raw progress.

⚠ Clamped into `[0, whole)` rather than trusted, for the reason
`clock_restore` clamps: a carry at or past a whole unit is a state
`bank_gain` can never leave behind, and accepting one would release
a unit nothing paid for.

api.sig: pub fn bank_restore_fraction(b: Bank, units: float, whole: integer)
api.doc:
Put a bank back from a fraction of a whole unit — `bank_fraction`'s
other half.

api.sig: pub fn bank_reset(b: Bank)
api.doc:
Throw the carry away.

⚠ **Deliberately a door of its own rather than `bank_restore(b, 0)`,
because it is a DECISION.**  A helper that comes back from recovery
is a repaired vehicle rather than the wreck that was carried in, so
its banked ground goes with the damage; an enemy that is merely
blocked keeps everything.  Two behaviours, and the one that discards
says so by name.

api.sig: pub struct TickClock
api.doc:
A fixed step and the time banked toward the next one.

⚠ **Both integers, and that is the whole file.**  `banked` is always
in `[0, step)` between calls, so there is no rounding to accumulate
and no epsilon to get the direction of wrong (`CLAUDE.md` § Timers
and epsilons: *neither direction is safe*).

api.sig: pub fn clock_new(step: integer) -> TickClock
api.doc:
A clock ticking every `step` base units.

⚠ **One argument, and a clock nobody configures behaves exactly as
dryopea's did before this file** — uncapped, unscaled, carrying its
remainder.  `plans/26` § The two rules under all of it: *defaults
mean the behaviour you already had*.

⚠ A step below 1 is clamped to 1 rather than refused, because the
alternative is a nullable clock at every call site for a case no
caller has: `clock_new(0)` is a mistake, not a mode.

api.sig: pub fn clock_units_from_micros(us: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Convert wall-clock microseconds — what loft's `ticks()` answers — to
this clock's base units.

⚠ **A multiplication, so it is exact.**  `main.loft` used to divide
microseconds by 1e6 into float seconds before the simulation saw
them, which threw the exactness away at the boundary and is half of
what plan 26 was opened for (`plans/26` § 1).

api.sig: pub fn clock_seconds_from_units(units: integer) -> float
api.doc:
The other direction, in SECONDS.

⚠⚠ **The seam plan 26 L3 was going to CLOSE, and what it did instead
was change hands.**  Before L3 every one-shot timer in the game came
through here to count float seconds — the boost and its cooldown, 90
ticks of helper recovery, 20 s of tower rebuild, the wave lull — and
`tick_timer.loft` took all four into integer units.  What is left is
not simulation at all:

* **authoring** — `emit.loft` writes a captured situation as
`.keys` text and a person reads it, and *seconds* is the unit a
person authors in.  Exactly `bank_fraction`'s position one family
over, and exactly as exact: a duration is a whole number of base
units, so the round trip through `clock_units_from_seconds`
recovers the integer this answered.
* **presentation** — the camera's ease is `1 − e^(−k·dt)` over real
frame time and is float by nature (`plans/26` § The invariant).

⚠ **No mover and no timer may call this.**  A mover that did would be
throwing away what `bank_gain` was built to keep, and a timer that did
would be re-introducing the direction problem `tick_timer.loft` exists
to delete.

api.sig: pub fn clock_units_from_seconds(seconds: float) -> integer
api.doc:
Float seconds to base units, ROUNDED — the authoring door's other
half.

⚠ **Rounding rather than truncating, for `tests/26_l1`'s reason one
layer out**: a float second's worth of units is a hair over or under
its exact count, and truncating a hair-under value costs a whole unit
at every boundary.  The error is ~1e-10 against a step of 2 000 000.

⚠ Negative time answers 0 rather than a negative count — the same
refusal `clock_advance` makes, stated here too because the rounding
would otherwise turn a small negative into `-0.5` and then into 0 by
accident rather than by rule.

api.sig: pub fn clock_set_rate(clk: TickClock, num: integer, den: integer)
api.doc:
Run simulated time at `num / den` of wall time.

⚠ **A RATIONAL rather than a float, and that is the whole reason it
needs no epsilon.**  `clock_set_rate(clk, 1, 3)` is a third of speed
exactly, for ever: a frame worth 100 units contributes 33 and the
leftover 1/3 is carried, where `elapsed * 0.3333…` drifts against a
rate it could not state in the first place.  Same distinction
`tick_bank.loft` § THE RATE IS SCALED AND THE TIME IS NOT draws one
family over — except that a clock's rate is authored by a KEYPRESS
rather than by `numbers.json`, so it is exact rather than quantised.

⚠ **Pause is `0 / 1`**, and it banks nothing while keeping what is
banked — so unpausing resumes mid-step rather than re-phasing the
simulation.  A step of 0 is a mistake, never a pause
(`clock_new`).

⚠ A negative `num` is clamped to 0 rather than rewinding.  Time
going backwards is dropped everywhere else in this file, and a rate
that ran the simulation in reverse would need every consumer to have
an inverse tick.

⚠ **Changing the rate DROPS the wall carry**, because the carry is
measured in `den`-ths of a base unit and the old `den` is gone.  It
is under one base unit — a third of a microsecond — and a rate
change is an event a player caused, not a per-frame path.
Example: @FIX-007

api.sig: pub fn clock_rate_num(clk: const TickClock) -> integer
api.doc: The rate's numerator — 0 for a paused clock.

api.sig: pub fn clock_rate_den(clk: const TickClock) -> integer
api.doc: The rate's denominator — never 0, and 1 for an unconfigured clock.

api.sig: pub fn clock_advance(clk: TickClock, elapsed: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Spend elapsed time, and answer the whole steps it bought.

⚠ **Integer division, not a subtraction loop.**  The loop is what
lost the tick — eleven subtractions of a repeating fraction leave a
remainder a hair under the twelfth — and it is also O(steps), so a
frame that delivered an hour walked five thousand iterations to say
so.  One division answers both.

⚠ **Time going backwards is DROPPED, not banked.**  A negative
elapsed is a clock that was reset or a caller subtracting in the
wrong order; banking it would owe the simulation negative ticks and
then swallow the next real frame.  Answering 0 and keeping the bank
is the only behaviour that cannot corrupt a run.

⚠ **No cap, and `clock_advance_capped` is the door that has one.**
A frame that delivers 20 s buys 30 ticks here, which is the property
dryopea's 654 gate measurements rest on.
Example: @FIX-001

api.sig: pub fn clock_advance_capped(clk: TickClock, elapsed: integer,
api.doc:
The same, for a driver that may have been backgrounded — at most
`max_steps`, and the excess is GONE.

⚠⚠ **It DROPS rather than defers, and the difference is the whole
door.**  `clock_advance` has already reduced the bank to the
sub-step remainder by the time this clamps, so the steps beyond the
cap are not owed: the next frame answers 1, not a burst.  The
tempting wrong version clamps the answer and leaves the backlog
banked, which runs the simulation behind the wall for ever after —
`tests/26_l4` § A cap that defers is that version, kept as the
control, and it is the only thing that makes this function's gate
non-trivial.

⚠ **And it must not compress**, which is moros's own note: *a
compressed catch-up is the variable-step bug wearing a bound's
clothes*.  Nothing here can — the step is fixed and this answers a
COUNT — but a driver that multiplied its tick's dt to "catch up"
would reintroduce exactly what `plans/22` § LOD is warned against.

⚠ A cap below 1 is clamped to 1, for `clock_new`'s reason: a cap of
zero is a simulation that can never advance, which is a mistake
rather than a mode.  Pause is a rate of 0.
Example: @FIX-004

api.sig: pub fn clock_pump(clk: TickClock, now: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Spend the time since the last reading of an ABSOLUTE wall clock.

⚠ **The server pump's door: it owns the wall and the caller owns no
subtraction.**  `now - last` written at the call site is where a
driver gets the order backwards once and silently swallows a frame —
`clock_advance` drops negative time, so the mistake looks like a
stutter rather than an error.

⚠ **The FIRST call primes and answers none.**  A pump whose first
reading was treated as elapsed would open a server with its whole
uptime as one burst of ticks.

⚠ **A wall going backwards re-primes** rather than dropping the
reading, because an absolute clock that jumped back is the new truth;
dropping it would owe every future pump the difference.

⚠ No cap — moros's server has none and `plans/26` § 3 says why the
two repos are both right.  A pump that needs one wraps this in the
same clamp `clock_advance_capped` applies.
Example: @FIX-003

api.sig: pub fn clock_step(_clk: const TickClock, n: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Ask for `n` steps, and answer how many that was.

⚠ **It does not touch the bank, and that is the whole point of it
being a separate door.**  A count is not elapsed time: a script
saying `tick 30` neither spends a live session's remainder nor
leaves one behind.  `play.loft` § TWO ways to ask made this
distinction one level up and measured what folding them costs.

⚠ It looks trivial and is not free to delete: without it a caller
that has a count must spell it as `n * step`, which is the exact
mistake `tests/19_p1` records — and which is only safe here because
the arithmetic is integer.  The door is what says so.

⚠⚠ **`_clk` IS UNDERSCORED BECAUSE IT IS UNREAD BY DESIGN, AND THE
UNDERSCORE IS LOAD-BEARING** (0.1.1).  Not reading it *is* the
contract — a count must not spend a live session's remainder — so
`never-read` is a true report of an intended fact rather than a
defect.  Left bare it fails the chunk's `LOFT_DENY_WARNINGS=1` CI,
and both tempting fixes are wrong: touching `clk` to quiet it breaks
the contract, and an `.allow_warnings` file switches the gate off for
every FUTURE warning in this package too.

⚠ **The parameter stays rather than the signature dropping it.**  A
caller holding a clock should reach for `clock_step(clk, n)` beside
`clock_advance(clk, elapsed)`; a bare `step(n)` would be an
arithmetic helper that names no case, and naming the case is the
entire reason this door exists.

Example: @FIX-002

api.sig: pub fn clock_step_units(clk: const TickClock) -> integer
api.doc: The step this clock ticks on, in base units.

api.sig: pub fn clock_banked(clk: const TickClock) -> integer
api.doc:
Time banked toward the next step, in base units — always in
`[0, step)`.

⚠ **Readable so a run can be RESTORED**, which is the whole of what
a rollback consumer needs from the timing half (`plans/26` § What
this plan does NOT build): re-running N steps from a restored bank
is bit-identical because `clock_step` is exact.
Example: @FIX-006

api.sig: pub fn clock_restore(clk: TickClock, banked: integer)
api.doc:
Put a clock back where it was — the other half of `clock_banked`.

⚠ Clamped into `[0, step)` rather than trusted: a bank at or past
the step is a state `clock_advance` can never leave behind, and
accepting one would make the next call answer a step nobody's time
paid for.

api.sig: pub fn clock_alpha(clk: const TickClock) -> float
api.doc:
How far the bank is toward the next step, in `[0, 1)`.

⚠ **The one number a renderer needs from a fixed-step clock**, and
the reason it is here rather than at the call site: `banked / step`
written by hand is a caller reaching INTO the accumulator, and a
caller that can read `banked` can also write it.  This is the read
door, and `clock_banked` (raw units, for save/restore) is the other
one — two questions, two answers, one field.

⚠ **Half-open by construction, not by a clamp.**  `clock_advance`
leaves `banked` in `[0, step)` and `clock_restore` refuses anything
else, so the division cannot reach 1.0 — which is what a caller
lerping between two states depends on: an alpha of exactly 1.0 would
draw the NEXT state one frame early, on the frame before the tick
that produces it.

⚠⚠ **What a consumer does with it is a PRESENTATION decision and this
file must not make it.**  The textbook use is
`lerp(previous_state, current_state, alpha)` — and dryopea measured it
against two alternatives over one drive (`tests/26_l5_the_alpha.loft`,
`@M035`):

* `lerp(prev, cur, alpha)` draws the step that has ALREADY happened,
so it is **exactly one step behind, for ever** — 2.598 m here,
because a step is 2/3 of a second;
* `cur + alpha·(cur − prev)` is **exact to machine precision** while
the velocity holds, and jumps a whole step's travel on the frame
the mover starts or stops;
* a first-order ease toward `cur` needs no previous state, lags
between the two, and is the only one whose picture depends on the
frames it was drawn on.

⚠ Three prices on three different axes, and which one is right is a
function of how long the STEP is — so a clock that picked one would be
wrong for every consumer whose step is a different length.  This
answers *where between two steps are we*; it does not answer *what
should be drawn there*.
Example: @FIX-005

api.sig: pub fn clock_drive(slow: TickClock, fast: const TickClock, n: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Spend `n` steps of `fast` on `slow`, and answer the slow steps that
bought.

⚠⚠ **The case is a strategy layer over a unit layer** — dryopea has
the shape twice already (the camera steps at frame rate while the sim
steps at 1.5 Hz, and `plans/22` § LOD contemplates ticking distant
things every N ticks).  ⚠ **And it is the OPPOSITE of that plan's
warning**: *bank progress, never multiply it* refuses to give a
distant enemy `N × dt` of movement in one tick.  This gives a slower
CLOCK the time those N ticks took, and it still ticks one step at a
time.

⚠ **Spelling it `n * step` at the call site is the shape of mistake
`tests/19_p1` records** — a count folded into a duration, wrong for
602 of the first 1000 `n`.  Here it is exact, because both sides are
integers; the door exists so that the next consumer does not
re-derive it in seconds and find out the hard way, and
`tests/26_l4` § Composing by hand is exact says so out loud rather
than letting this comment overclaim.

⚠ **A slow clock driven this way LAGS its driver by less than one
fast step, and never leads.**  The fast clock's own bank is time
that has not become a tick yet, so it has not been handed on — which
is the correct answer and not an approximation: the composed clock is
exactly as far along as the ticks that actually happened.

⚠ **`slow`'s own rate still applies.**  A rate set on both clocks
multiplies, which is a composition a caller asked for; set it on the
one that faces the wall.
Example: @FIX-008

api.sig: pub struct Timer
api.doc:
A one-shot duration and how much of it has been spent.

⚠ **Both integers, and `total == 0` is UNARMED** — the zero-default
that makes a partial struct literal correct everywhere this replaces
a `0.0` seconds field.  See the header.

api.sig: pub fn timer_new() -> Timer
api.doc: A timer nobody has armed.

api.sig: pub fn timer_armed(units: integer) -> Timer
api.doc:
A timer armed for `units` — the factory, for a struct literal that
wants one already running.

⚠ `Enemy`'s pre-walk window is the case: an enemy is built already
standing, so the field has to arrive armed.

api.sig: pub fn timer_arm(t: Timer, units: integer)
api.doc:
Arm it for `units`, from zero.

⚠ **A duration of zero or less DISARMS rather than firing.**  Both
readings are defensible and this one is what the call sites already
mean: a schedule authored with a lull of 0 sends the next wave
immediately because nothing is running, not because a timer fired.
⚠ It also re-arms from wherever it was, so a boost pressed during a
boost restarts the clock rather than extending it — the behaviour the
float version had, stated rather than inherited.
Example: @FIX-011

api.sig: pub fn timer_running(t: const Timer) -> boolean
api.doc: Is this timer running — armed, and not yet fired?

api.sig: pub fn timer_left(t: const Timer) -> integer
api.doc:
Base units still to go.  Zero for a timer that is not running.

⚠ **The DOWN reading**, and it is a subtraction rather than a second
field.  `helper.recover` and `Vehicle.boost_left` were both stored
this way and each carried its own epsilon; there is one number now
and it is exact.

api.sig: pub fn timer_spent(t: const Timer) -> integer
api.doc:
Base units gone by.  Zero for a timer that is not running.

⚠ **The UP reading**, off the same number.  `TowerCharge.repair` was
stored this way — *seconds banked toward the rebuild* — because zero
had to mean "nobody is working on it", and that is still what an
unarmed timer says.

api.sig: pub fn timer_total(t: const Timer) -> integer
api.doc: The whole duration this timer was armed for, in base units.

api.sig: pub fn timer_fraction(t: const Timer) -> float
api.doc:
How far through it is, in `[0, 1)` — 0.0 for a timer that is not
running.

⚠ **The presentation door, and the one place a float appears** — a
HUD showing a rebuild part-done, exactly `bank_fraction`'s position
one family over.  Nothing in the simulation may read it: a
comparison against 1.0 here is the epsilon problem walking back in
through the display.

api.sig: pub fn timer_spend(t: Timer, units: integer) -> boolean
api.doc:
Spend `units` of it.  Answers whether THIS call finished it.

⚠ **It fires exactly once and then disarms**, which is the whole
difference from `bank_gain`: the remainder past the boundary is
DISCARDED, because a one-shot's residue means nothing afterwards.
Carrying it would make the next arming shorter than the one before —
measured in `tests/26_l3` § A one-shot built on a bank, where a 5.0 s
cooldown costs 8 ticks the first time and 7 the second.

⚠ A timer that is not running answers false and stays that way, so a
caller may spend into it unconditionally — which is what
`vehicle_burn` does with the cooldown every single tick.

⚠ Non-positive time is dropped rather than owed, for
`clock_advance`'s reason: time going backwards must not un-fire
anything.
Example: @FIX-011

api.sig: pub fn timer_cancel(t: Timer)
api.doc:
Stop it without firing.

⚠ **A door of its own rather than `timer_arm(t, 0)`, because it is a
DECISION** — the same argument `bank_reset` makes.  A vehicle that
respawns loses the boost it was in the middle of; a cooldown that is
merely running keeps everything.  Two behaviours, and the one that
throws work away says so by name.

api.sig: pub fn timer_restore_left(t: Timer, left: integer, total: integer)
api.doc:
Put a timer back from a DOWN reading — `units` left of `total`.

⚠ Clamped rather than trusted, for `clock_restore`'s reason: `left`
past `total` is a state `timer_spend` can never leave behind, and a
`left` of zero or less is a timer that has already fired, which is an
unarmed one.

api.sig: pub fn timer_restore_spent(t: Timer, spent: integer, total: integer)
api.doc:
Put a timer back from an UP reading — `units` spent of `total`.

⚠ The other half, and the two are not interchangeable at the call
site: `emit.loft` writes whichever reading its field was authored in,
so a tower's rebuild round-trips as *banked* and a helper's recovery
as *left*.

stage.description: A retained 2-D scene for loft: a node tree you mutate, with transforms, clipping, batching, pointer routing and widget states

api.sig: pub struct StageNode
api.doc:
A node's local placement, plus the world affine `compose` derives for it.

⚠ NAMED `StageNode` AND NOT `Node`, because a type name is GLOBAL across the
dependency graph and `mesh3d` — which `graphics` pulls in — already publishes a
`Node` for its 3-D scene.  The compiler refuses the collision outright rather
than resolving it silently, which is the good outcome; the cost of finding it
after publishing would have been a rename nobody can make.

The affine is 2x3 and is applied as
x' = a*lx + c*ly + tx
y' = b*lx + d*ly + ty
which is the layout the instanced draw path consumes unchanged.

api.sig: pub struct Layer
api.doc:
Everything one ordering band carries: how much of the camera it feels, what
atmosphere stands in front of it, and how far out of focus it is.

⚠ ONE RECORD, NOT THREE PARALLEL VECTORS.  Parallax lived in a bare
`vector<float>` and fog and blur were about to join it as siblings — which is
exactly the shape that put a sequence's name on another sequence's cells in
P5: every list stays well-formed on its own and only the correspondence goes
wrong, silently.  A layer's facts travel together.

api.sig: pub struct View
api.doc:
A way of LOOKING at the stage: a camera and the screen rect it paints into.

⚠ A VIEW IS PRESENTATION, NEVER WORLD.  The scene cannot tell how many are
looking at it — which is the split this phase exists to enforce: the world is
deterministic and shared, the presentation is local and free.  Window size,
camera and ambient motion may differ per viewer and must be allowed to.

api.sig: pub struct StageLight
api.doc:
A point light: where it stands, how far it reaches, and what colour it casts.

⚠ IT LIVES IN WORLD SPACE, like everything else the app places.  A light is
not attached to a node, so moving a torch-bearer means moving the light too —
deliberate, because a light parented to a sprite would inherit that sprite's
rotation and scale, and neither means anything to a point light.
⚠ `StageLight`, not `Light`: a TYPE name is global across every package in the
build, and `mesh3d` — pulled in by `graphics` — already publishes a `Light`.
The compiler refusing is the good outcome; after publishing, this rename is one
nobody can make.  Same reason the node is `StageNode`.

api.sig: pub struct Stage
pub struct Sequence
api.doc:
A run of atlas cells played at a rate.

⚠ THE NAME LIVES HERE, not in a list beside `st_seqs`.  A parallel vector that
only the naming registrar appended to drifted the moment a caller mixed
`add_sequence` with `add_named_sequence`, and every later name then pointed at
somebody else's cells — silently, because both lists were individually
well-formed.  One home per fact; the test that caught it is kept.

api.sig: pub struct Mask
api.doc:
An alpha mask: per-texel coverage, row-major, 0..255.

A sprite is mostly holes, so a rect test answers the wrong question — you can
SEE through a tree, therefore you must be able to CLICK through it.  A node
without a mask is solid, which is the right default for a panel or a tile.

api.sig: pub struct Place
api.doc:
Where to put a node, and how.  A struct rather than nine parameters because the
compiler said so — `too-many-parameters` fires at eight, and a caller's burden
is fixed by a struct where a reader's is fixed by an extracted function.

⚠ THE DEFAULTS ARE THE POINT, not convenience.  Scale defaults to 1.0 and not to
the zero an omitted field would otherwise take: a scale of 0 is a *meaningful*
value of the field's domain — it collapses the node to nothing — so an author
who writes `Place { pl_x: 10.0, pl_y: 20.0 }` and gets an invisible node has
been handed a legal answer to a question they did not ask.  That is exactly the
case `omitted-field-zero` exists to warn about, answered here at the declaration.

api.sig: pub struct Bounds
api.doc:
A point, so a caller can ask where something ended up without unpacking six
floats.  `world_point` is the only honest way to check a transform: a matrix
means nothing except through what it does to a point.

api.sig: pub struct P2
pub fn stage_new() -> Stage
pub fn node_count(self: const Stage) -> integer
pub fn node_add(self: Stage, parent: integer, p: const Place) -> integer
api.doc:
Add a node and answer its index.  `parent` is -1 for a root.

⚠ Refuses a forward parent reference by answering -1.  `compose` is a single
forward pass, so a child placed before its parent would read an unwritten world
transform — silently, and the frame would look almost right.
Example: @STG-002 — the tree is a flat array and a forward parent reference is
refused, because `compose` is a single forward pass that would otherwise read an
unwritten parent and answer plausibly.

api.sig: pub fn compose(self: Stage)
api.doc:
Derive every node's world affine in one forward pass.

A node's local transform is  T(x, y) . R(rot) . S(sx, sy) . T(-ox, -oy), which
is what makes the ORIGIN the anchor: the local point (ox, oy) maps exactly to
(x, y), so a sprite whose origin sits at its feet stands up from where it is
placed.  World = parent's world composed with that.
Example: @STG-003 — deriving is the caller's to trigger; skipping it renders the
previous state, which reads as input lag rather than as a missing call.

api.sig: pub fn depth_cue(self: Stage, near: float, far: float, far_scale: float,
api.doc:
Turn the depth cue on.  `near` and `far` are depths; a node at `far` is drawn at
`far_scale` of its size and hazed `far_haze` toward `haze_colour`, and one at
`near` is untouched.  Off by default, and off means an identical picture.

This is the 2.5-D FEEL: distance reads as smaller and less distinct, which is
what separates a mob standing behind a wall from one standing in front of it
even when neither overlaps the other.  Real blur belongs to the per-layer pass;
a haze toward the fog colour costs one lerp and carries most of the effect.

api.sig: pub fn cue_of(self: const Stage, depth: float) -> float
api.doc:
How far through the cue a depth sits: 0 at the near plane, 1 at the far one,
clamped outside them so a stray depth cannot invert the effect.

api.sig: pub fn haze_of(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> float
api.doc: How hazed node `idx` is, 0..1 — what a renderer fades toward the haze colour.

api.sig: pub fn order(self: const Stage) -> vector<integer>
api.doc: The draw order, derived by `compose`: indices, back to front.

api.sig: pub fn bounds_of(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> Bounds
api.doc:
A node's axis-aligned bounds in world space.
Example: @STG-007 — a clip inherits, intersects, and is axis-aligned.

⚠ AXIS-ALIGNED, so a ROTATED clipper clips to its bounding box rather than to
its turned rectangle.  A scissor is axis-aligned in hardware and there is no
honest way to make it otherwise; a rotated clip needs a stencil, which this arc
does not have.  Stated rather than discovered.

api.sig: pub fn world_point(self: const Stage, idx: integer, lx: float, ly: float) -> P2
api.doc:
Where a point in node `idx`'s own space lands in world space.  Valid after
`compose`; answers (0, 0) for an index that is not a node.

api.sig: pub fn world_origin(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> P2
api.doc:
Where the node's ORIGIN is — the point A7's depth key sorts on.
Example: @STG-001 — a node is anchored by its origin, so a sprite whose origin
sits at its feet stands up from where it was placed.

api.sig: pub struct UiRect
api.doc:
── A2: the draw list ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

⚠ THESE THREE TYPES ARE NOT NEW.  Their field names and types are copied
EXACTLY from `lavition_ui`, which produces `vector<DrawRect>` from
`panel_draw_list` today and is proven by a 12 k-line editor.  Matching a working
command shape rather than minting a rival one is the whole point: a game's UI
and an editor's UI have to reach the GPU by one path, or the batcher sees two.

⚠ AND THEY NEED ONE HOME, WHICH THEY DO NOT YET HAVE.  `lavition_ui` is
unpublished, so its `DrawRect` and this one are two nominal types with one
shape.  Until it is published (@PLN145 `D0`) the types cannot literally be
shared, and one of the two must eventually give — see the plan.

api.sig: pub struct DrawRect
api.doc: A packed 0xRRGGBB colour, as `lavition_ui` carries it.

api.sig: pub struct DrawText
pub fn draw_list(self: const Stage) -> vector<DrawRect>
api.doc:
Emit the scene as a flat command list, in index order.

Index order IS the draw order for now: `A4` gives depth its own key, and doing
it here would be a second ordering rule to keep in step with that one.  A node
with no area emits nothing — a zero size is how a pure transform parent says it
is scaffolding rather than a thing to look at.

api.sig: pub fn render(list: const vector<DrawRect>, cv: graphics::Canvas)
api.doc:
Paint a command list onto a software canvas.

⚠ THE ALPHA BYTE IS ADDED HERE, and it has to be.  A `DrawRect` carries
0xRRGGBB — `lavition_ui` says so, and keeps it a plain integer so it needs no
graphics dependency — while `graphics::Canvas` reads 0xAARRGGBB and treats a
missing top byte as FULLY TRANSPARENT.  That is graphics' own trap: the colour
looks right in the source and paints nothing.  One `| 0xff000000` at the
boundary is the whole fix, and it belongs at the boundary rather than in every
caller.

Example: @GFX-001

api.sig: pub fn opaque(colour: integer) -> integer
api.doc: 0xRRGGBB -> 0xAARRGGBB, leaving an already-opaque colour alone.

api.sig: pub struct Batch
api.doc: One run of consecutive instances that share an atlas.

api.sig: pub fn batches(self: const Stage) -> vector<Batch>
api.doc:
Split the visible nodes into runs, in scene order.
Example: @STG-004 — adjacent runs only, never sorted, and what the interleave
costs: four sprites across two atlases are four draws, cured by packing.

api.sig: pub fn pack_instances(self: const Stage) -> vector<single>
api.doc:
Pack every visible node into one instance buffer, in the same order `batches`
counted.  The two walk the scene by the same rule, so a batch's `b_first` and
`b_count` index this buffer directly.

api.sig: pub struct Painter
api.doc: The GL objects a stage needs, built once.

api.sig: pub fn painter_new() -> Painter
api.doc: Compile the shader and upload the unit quad.  Call once, after a window exists.

api.sig: pub fn gl_render(self: Stage, p: Painter, screen_w: float, screen_h: float) -> integer
api.doc:
Draw the scene, one instanced call per run.  Answers the number of draw calls
issued, which is the half of the gate that pixels cannot see: a batch that fell
back to one draw per sprite would look identical and cost N.

api.sig: pub fn scissor_of(self: const Stage, view: integer, b: const Batch, coff: const P2) -> Bounds
api.doc:
The screen rect a run may paint in: the view's own rect, intersected with the
batch's clip once that clip is moved by the same offset as its content.

An unbounded rect is spelled as the whole target rather than as a flag, so the
intersection is arithmetic in every case and the unsplit stage is the
degenerate cell rather than a second path.

api.sig: pub fn add_mask(self: Stage, w: integer, h: integer, alpha: const vector<integer>) -> integer
api.doc: Register an alpha mask and answer its index, for `Place.pl_mask`.

api.sig: pub fn to_local(self: const Stage, idx: integer, sx: float, sy: float) -> P2
api.doc:
Take a screen point into node `idx`'s own space.

The world affine is 2x2 plus a translation, so the inverse is closed form —
`det = a*d - c*b`, and no general 4x4 inversion is involved.  A degenerate node
(zero scale) has no inverse and answers its own origin rather than an infinity.

api.sig: pub fn hits(self: const Stage, idx: integer, sx: float, sy: float) -> boolean
api.doc:
Is this screen point ON node `idx` — inside its rect AND, where it has a mask,
on a texel that is not a hole?

api.sig: pub fn pick(self: const Stage, sx: float, sy: float) -> integer
api.doc:
The topmost node under this screen point, or -1.
Example: @STG-006 — picking samples alpha, so a click falls through a hole.

Walks the draw order BACKWARDS, so the node drawn last — the one on top — is
tested first, and insertion order breaks a tie the same way it does when
drawing.  One order, two consumers: a pick that disagreed with the picture
would be worse than no pick at all.

api.sig: pub fn press(self: Stage, sx: float, sy: float) -> integer
api.doc: A press picks, and REMEMBERS.

api.sig: pub fn release(self: Stage, sx: float, sy: float) -> integer
api.doc:
A release answers the node that took the PRESS, wherever the pointer is now.
Example: @STG-005 — why a hit test alone is not input routing.

⚠ THE CAPTURE IS THE POINT, and it is the half everyone forgets.  Without it a
button fires when you press it and slide away, and never fires when you press it
and drift a pixel — both of which feel broken and neither of which a rect test
can explain.  A release with nothing captured answers -1.

api.sig: pub fn released_on(self: const Stage, idx: integer, sx: float, sy: float) -> boolean
api.doc:
Did the release land on the node that was pressed?  A button fires only when
this is true; `release` still reports the captured node either way.

api.sig: pub fn capture(self: const Stage) -> integer
pub enum UiState
api.doc:
The four states a widget node can be in.

⚠ `Disabled` outranks the other three: a node that cannot be used must not
look pressable even while the pointer is on it.

api.sig: pub fn set_pointer(self: Stage, kind: integer)
api.doc: Say whether the pointer is a mouse or a finger.  Mouse is the default.

api.sig: pub fn pointer(self: const Stage) -> integer
pub fn pointer_move(self: Stage, sx: float, sy: float)
api.doc: The pointer moved without a button.  A touch stream never sends this.

api.sig: pub fn hovered(self: const Stage) -> integer
api.doc:
The node the pointer is over, or -1.  Answers even under touch, where it is
the node the finger is ON — `ui_state` is what declines to call that `Over`.

api.sig: pub fn set_enabled(self: Stage, idx: integer, on: boolean)
api.doc: Take a node out of use, or put it back.

api.sig: pub fn enabled(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> boolean
pub fn ui_state(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> UiState
api.doc: What this node looks like right now.

api.sig: pub fn click(self: Stage, sx: float, sy: float) -> integer
api.doc:
The release door for a widget: answers the node that FIRES, or -1.

⚠ **Use this OR `release`, not both** — either ends the press.  `release`
answers *who took the press* and leaves the fired/not decision to the caller;
this answers the question a button actually asks.  It exists because combining
`release` with `released_on` by hand is where press-then-leave-then-release
goes wrong, and that is a mistake a library can simply not offer.

api.sig: pub fn focusable(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> boolean
api.doc: Can this node hold the keyboard?

api.sig: pub fn set_focusable(self: Stage, idx: integer, on: boolean)
pub fn focused(self: const Stage) -> integer
api.doc: Which node has the keyboard, or -1.

api.sig: pub fn set_focus(self: Stage, idx: integer)
api.doc:
Give it the keyboard.  A node that cannot take it clears the focus instead, so
this never leaves the keyboard somewhere unreachable.

api.sig: pub fn focus_next(self: Stage)
api.doc:
⚠ TAB ORDER IS THE DECLARED ORDER — the order the nodes were added, which is
the order a reader of the building code sees.  A separate `tab_index` would be
a second ordering to keep in step with the first, and the two disagree the
moment someone inserts a node.

api.sig: pub fn focus_prev(self: Stage)
pub fn set_field(self: Stage, idx: integer, s: text)
api.doc: Make this node an editable field holding `s`, and give it the tab order.

api.sig: pub fn is_field(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> boolean
pub fn field_text(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> text
pub fn field_caret(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> integer
api.doc: Where the caret is, counted in CHARACTERS.

api.sig: pub fn field_mark(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> integer
api.doc: The selection anchor.  Equal to the caret when nothing is selected.

api.sig: pub fn field_selection(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> text
api.doc: The selected text, or "" when the caret is a point.

api.sig: pub fn field_place_caret(self: Stage, idx: integer, at_char: integer, extend: boolean)
api.doc:
Put the caret at a CHARACTER index — what a click resolves to once whoever
draws the text has turned an x-coordinate into a count.

api.sig: pub fn clipboard(self: const Stage) -> text
api.doc: Our own clipboard — see the header.

api.sig: pub fn set_clipboard(self: Stage, s: text)
pub fn text_event(self: Stage, s: text)
api.doc:
Commit text into the focused field, replacing any selection.

⚠ This is where IME text arrives: `EV_TEXT` delivers a whole COMMITTED string,
which may be several characters and is very often not ASCII.

api.sig: pub fn key_event(self: Stage, key: integer, mods: integer)
api.doc:
A key, with the modifiers that arrived WITH it.  Tab moves the focus; every
other key goes to the focused field.

api.sig: pub fn render_stage(self: const Stage, cv: graphics::Canvas)
api.doc:
Paint the scene onto a software canvas, honouring each node's alpha and tint.

`render(list, canvas)` stays the path for a `lavition_ui` command list, which
carries 0xRRGGBB and no alpha by design.  This is the stage's own path, where a
node has an alpha to respect — and the two must agree wherever alpha is 1.

api.sig: pub fn render_view(self: const Stage, view: integer, cv: graphics::Canvas)
api.doc:
Paint one VIEW of the scene: the same nodes, through that view's camera, and
confined to its own screen rect.

⚠ THE VIEWPORT NARROWS THE SPAN, it does not test each pixel — the same
technique A6's clip uses, so the boundary falls where the arithmetic puts it
rather than where a per-pixel predicate rounds it, and the two cannot disagree
about a shared edge.

api.sig: pub fn set_camera(self: Stage, x: float, y: float)
api.doc:
Move the camera.  Does NOT dirty the instance buffer — that is the point.

An unsplit stage IS a one-view stage, so this is view 0's camera rather than a
second place a camera can live — the same move P2 made with parallax, where
flat scrolling is every factor at 1.0 instead of a separate path.

api.sig: pub fn camera_x(self: const Stage) -> float
pub fn camera_y(self: const Stage) -> float
pub fn set_parallax(self: Stage, layer: integer, factor: float)
api.doc:
How much of the camera a layer feels.  1.0 is the world; below that is a
background that lags; above it a foreground that leads.  Flat scrolling is every
factor at 1.0, which is the degenerate case rather than a second code path.

api.sig: pub fn parallax_of(self: const Stage, layer: integer) -> float
pub fn cam_offset(self: const Stage, layer: integer) -> P2
api.doc: The screen-space offset a layer's content is drawn at, in view 0.

api.sig: pub fn uploads(self: const Stage) -> integer
api.doc:
How many times the instance buffer has been written.  A pure camera move must
not move this — the property the whole design turns on.

api.sig: pub fn set_time(self: Stage, t: float)
api.doc:
Example: @STG-008 — ambient motion is free, out of step, and visual only.
Advance the ambient clock.  Does NOT dirty the instance buffer — that is the
whole point of deriving the phase rather than stepping it.

api.sig: pub fn time_of(self: const Stage) -> float
pub fn sway_of(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> float
api.doc:
How far node `idx` is displaced right now, in pixels.  Bounded by its amplitude
by construction, since it is an amplitude times a sine.

api.sig: pub fn add_sequence(self: Stage, first: integer, count: integer, fps: float,
api.doc: Register a sequence and answer its index, for `Place.pl_seq`.

api.sig: pub fn advance(self: Stage, dt_us: integer)
api.doc:
Step every animated node by `dt_us` MICROSECONDS — the simulation's own delta,
not a clock this library reads.

⚠ Dirties the instance buffer, unlike the camera and the ambient clock — an
animated sprite genuinely changes one number per frame.  That number is a FRAME
INDEX and not a uv rect, so it is one float and not four.

api.sig: pub fn frame_of(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> integer
api.doc: Which cell node `idx` shows right now.

api.sig: pub fn restart(self: Stage, idx: integer)
api.doc: Reset a node to the start of its sequence.

api.sig: pub enum Prop
api.doc:
Which of a node's numbers a tween drives.

⚠ Every one is a `float` the node already stores.  Colour, atlas and the
sequence are not here on purpose: they are not numbers you can be *half way*
between, and interpolating them would produce values the node never holds.

api.sig: pub fn prop_of(self: const Stage, idx: integer, p: Prop) -> float
api.doc: What that property reads right now.

api.sig: pub fn set_prop(self: Stage, idx: integer, p: Prop, v: float)
api.doc:
Write it now.  The immediate door — the tween door writes through the same
switch, one frame at a time.

api.sig: pub fn tween_prop(self: Stage, idx: integer, p: Prop, to: float, dur_us: integer,
api.doc:
Move `p` from where it is now to `to`, over `dur_us` microseconds.

⚠ `from` is read at THIS moment, so a tween started mid-flight carries on from
where the last one had got to rather than snapping back to a remembered start.
Replaces any tween already on this (node, property).

api.sig: pub fn prop_tweening(self: const Stage, idx: integer, p: Prop) -> boolean
api.doc: Is that property still moving?

api.sig: pub fn cancel_prop_tween(self: Stage, idx: integer, p: Prop)
api.doc: Stop it wherever it has got to.  The property keeps its current value.

api.sig: pub fn cancel_node_tweens(self: Stage, idx: integer)
api.doc: Drop every tween on a node.

api.sig: pub fn tween_count(self: const Stage) -> integer
api.doc: How many property tweens the stage is holding — the gate reads this.

api.sig: pub fn set_projection(self: Stage, mode: integer)
pub fn projection(self: const Stage) -> integer
pub fn sequence_count(self: const Stage) -> integer
pub fn add_named_sequence(self: Stage, name: text, first: integer, count: integer,
api.doc:
Register a sequence under a NAME, so `face` and `set_action` can resolve it.
The convention is `<key>`, `<key>_<action>`, `<key>_<action>_<facing>`, and
resolution walks it most-specific first.

api.sig: pub fn facing_name(angle: float) -> text
api.doc:
Which of the four compass facings an angle points at.

⚠ SCREEN SPACE, Y DOWN: angle 0 is +x (east) and +pi/2 is +y (south), matching
`pl_rot` and the shader.  The edges are HALF-OPEN, as A4's picking rects are —
45 degrees belongs to south — so no angle is claimed by two facings.

api.sig: pub fn face(self: Stage, idx: integer, angle: float)
api.doc: Point a node at `angle` radians.  Top-down turns it; side-on picks and flips.

api.sig: pub fn set_action(self: Stage, idx: integer, action: text)
api.doc: What a node is doing — "idle", "walk", "attack".  Re-resolves, phase intact.

api.sig: pub fn facing_of(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> float
pub fn action_of(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> text
pub fn rotation_of(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> float
api.doc: The sprite's own rotation, which side-on leaves alone.

api.sig: pub fn mirrored(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> boolean
pub fn view_count(self: const Stage) -> integer
pub fn add_view(self: Stage, x: integer, y: integer, w: integer,
api.doc:
Add a view painting into the screen rect `(x, y, w, h)`.  A width of 0 or less
means unbounded — the whole target, which is what view 0 starts as.

api.sig: pub fn set_view_rect(self: Stage, view: integer, x: integer, y: integer,
pub fn set_view_camera(self: Stage, view: integer, x: float, y: float)
api.doc: Move one view's camera.  Like `set_camera`, it does not dirty the buffer.

api.sig: pub fn view_camera_x(self: const Stage, view: integer) -> float
pub fn view_camera_y(self: const Stage, view: integer) -> float
pub fn view_offset(self: const Stage, view: integer, layer: integer) -> P2
api.doc:
Where a layer's content lands on screen in this view: the camera un-applied by
the layer's parallax, then moved into the view's rect.

⚠ THE VIEWPORT ORIGIN IS PART OF THE MAPPING, not decoration.  Leave it out and
both views draw on top of each other while every camera test still passes.

api.sig: pub fn sync_instances(self: Stage) -> boolean
api.doc:
Pack the instance buffer if the scene changed, and say whether it did.

One home for *when does the buffer get rewritten*, so the GL path and any
count of uploads cannot disagree about it — and so N views can be shown to
cost ONE upload without a GL context to prove it in.

api.sig: pub fn pick_in(self: const Stage, view: integer, sx: float, sy: float) -> integer
api.doc:
The topmost node under a screen point AS THAT VIEW SEES IT, or -1.

⚠ ONE SCREEN POINT IS A DIFFERENT WORLD POINT IN EACH VIEW — the same reason
P2 un-applies the camera per LAYER.  A point outside the view's own rect is
not that view's to answer, whatever its camera would map it to.

api.sig: pub fn in_view_rect(self: const Stage, view: integer, sx: float, sy: float) -> boolean
api.doc:
Is this screen point inside the view's rect?  An unbounded view holds every
point, which is what keeps the unsplit stage a single code path.

api.sig: pub fn hits_in(self: const Stage, view: integer, idx: integer, sx: float,
api.doc: Does this node cover the screen point, as `view` maps it?

api.sig: pub fn add_light(self: Stage, x: float, y: float, radius: float, colour: integer,
api.doc: Add a light.  Answers its index, for `move_light`.

api.sig: pub fn move_light(self: Stage, i: integer, x: float, y: float)
pub fn light_count(self: const Stage) -> integer
pub fn set_ambient(self: Stage, level: float)
api.doc:
How lit the world is before any light: 1.0 leaves the material untouched, so a
game that never asks for light cannot be dimmed by this existing.  Turn it
down and the scene goes dark except where a light reaches.

api.sig: pub fn ambient(self: const Stage) -> float
pub fn light_reach(l: const StageLight, px: float, py: float) -> float
api.doc:
What a light contributes at a point: linear in the radius, clamped at both ends.

⚠ LINEAR, `1 - d/r`, and that is a design call.  This phase's gate is
hand-computed values, and a curve nobody can hand-compute is a gate nobody
maintains.  L2 owns the prettier curve, and its own gate says how: expectations
GENERATED from the same constants the shader uses, so retuning is one edit.

api.sig: pub fn lit_colour(self: const Stage, idx: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
The colour a node is actually drawn in: its material, multiplied by the light
standing on its footprint.

⚠ ONE HOME.  Both render paths and the instance packer read this rather than
each folding the light in themselves — the shape P6 shipped a defect through,
where one fact derived per path was validated only where the derivations
happened to agree.

api.sig: pub struct Lit
api.doc: A light level, per channel, 0..1.

api.sig: pub fn set_light_map(self: Stage, on: boolean)
pub fn light_map(self: const Stage) -> boolean
pub fn set_hud_layer(self: Stage, n: integer)
api.doc: Layers at or above `n` draw AFTER the composite and take no light.

api.sig: pub fn hud_layer(self: const Stage) -> integer
pub fn light_rgb_at(self: const Stage, wx: float, wy: float) -> Lit
api.doc:
The light standing at a world point, per channel.

⚠ THE ONE HOME both samplings read: L1 asks it at a sprite's origin, L2 asks
it per pixel.  One curve, one floor, one clamp — so the per-sprite and the
per-pixel answers cannot disagree about the same point.

api.sig: pub fn light_level_at(self: const Stage, wx: float, wy: float) -> float
api.doc:
The scalar level at a world point — the green channel of a white light, and
the number the monotonic-and-floored invariant is stated about.

api.sig: pub fn composite_light(self: const Stage, view: integer, cv: graphics::Canvas)
api.doc:
Multiply every pixel of the view's rect by the light standing there.

⚠ THE SCREEN IS MAPPED TO THE WORLD THROUGH THE WORLD PLANE — layer 0, the
plane lights live on.  A parallaxed background is therefore lit as though it
stood on that plane, which is the honest simplification here: per-layer
atmosphere is L3's question, not this pass's.

api.sig: pub fn composite_shader_source() -> text
api.doc:
The composite's fragment shader.  Public so a test can check it reads the
falloff and the floor as UNIFORMS rather than carrying its own copy of them.

api.sig: pub fn set_layer_fog(self: Stage, layer: integer, colour: integer, density: float)
api.doc: Fade this layer toward `colour`.  Density 0 is clear and changes nothing.

api.sig: pub fn layer_fog_colour(self: const Stage, layer: integer) -> integer
pub fn layer_fog_density(self: const Stage, layer: integer) -> float
pub fn set_layer_blur(self: Stage, layer: integer, radius: integer)
api.doc:
Put this layer out of focus by `radius` pixels.  0 is sharp.

⚠ THE BLUR RUNS WHEN THE LAYER FINISHES, so it softens everything drawn up to
and including it and NOTHING above — which is what makes a sharp foreground
over a hazy distance possible, and what a fullscreen blur cannot do.  Distant
bands therefore blur together, which is what *distance is out of focus* means.

api.sig: pub fn layer_blur(self: const Stage, layer: integer) -> integer
pub fn blur_region(cv: graphics::Canvas, x0: integer, y0: integer, x1: integer,
api.doc:
Box-blur a rectangle of the canvas in place.

⚠ SAMPLES ARE CLAMPED TO THE EDGE, never read as black.  Counting an
off-image sample as black loses light everywhere the kernel overhangs, and it
shows as a dark frame around the picture — the classic bug this phase gates
against.  Clamping keeps a uniform field EXACTLY itself.

text2d.description: Text that always draws — a built-in face, a glyph atlas, measured metrics, wrapping and alignment, with no font file and no GL context

api.sig: pub fn face_codes() -> vector<integer>
api.doc: The codepoints, ascending — `face_row` bisects this.

api.sig: pub fn face_rows() -> vector<integer>
api.doc: Seven rows per glyph, in the same order as `face_codes`.

api.sig: pub fn blit_glyph(cv: graphics::Canvas, code: integer, x: integer, y: integer,
api.doc:
Blit one codepoint's glyph with its top-left at (x, y).  Shared by the direct
blitter and by the atlas, so the bit-walk has ONE home and the two can never
disagree about what a glyph looks like.

api.sig: pub fn text_width(s: text, scale: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Width in pixels of `s` at scale 1, INCLUDING the single-pixel gap after every
glyph but the last.  Exact — the caller can centre with it and be right.

api.sig: pub fn line_height(scale: integer) -> integer
api.doc: Height of one line at `scale`.

api.sig: pub fn write_text(cv: graphics::Canvas, s: text, x: integer, y: integer,
api.doc:
⚠ NAMED `write_text`, NOT `draw_text`.  `graphics` already has `draw_text` as a
METHOD on `Canvas`, and a method spelling outranks a library's free function of
the same name (loft#940) — so a bare `draw_text(cv, …)` here resolves to the
seven-parameter GL one and fails at the call site with an arity error that names
neither library.  A distinct verb costs nothing and is reachable.

Draw `s` with its top-left at (x, y).  Answers the width drawn, so a caller can
lay out the next run without measuring twice.

⚠ Iterates CHARACTERS, not bytes.  `len(text)` counts characters and an indexed
read is bytes, so a byte loop truncates multi-byte text silently — the trap the
strict-index lint exists for.  A character with no glyph draws a blank of the
same width rather than being skipped, so a string never changes length because
one character was missing.

api.sig: pub fn write_centred(cv: graphics::Canvas, s: text, bx: integer, by: integer,
api.doc:
Draw `s` centred in the box (bx, by, bw, bh).  The commonest thing a HUD wants,
and the commonest place an off-by-one lands.

api.sig: pub struct Atlas
pub struct Quad
api.doc: One glyph placed on a line: where it goes, and which cell it comes from.

api.sig: pub fn atlas_new(scale: integer, capacity: integer) -> Atlas
api.doc:
A sheet with room for `capacity` glyphs at `scale`.  Shelf-packed in a grid,
which is enough for a fixed-width face — a proportional one would want a real
packer, and would still not change what the caller sees.

api.sig: pub fn atlas_glyph_count(self: const Atlas) -> integer
pub fn atlas_writes(self: const Atlas) -> integer
api.doc:
How many times the sheet has been WRITTEN.  A GL consumer uploads on exactly
these, so a caller can assert that a changing label costs no upload — which is
the property the whole arc exists for.

api.sig: pub fn atlas_cell(self: Atlas, code: integer) -> integer
api.doc: The cell holding `code`, rasterising it on first use.  -1 when the sheet is full.

api.sig: pub fn layout(self: Atlas, s: text, x: integer, y: integer) -> vector<Quad>
api.doc:
Lay a string out over the sheet.  Answers one quad per character; NOTHING is
written to the sheet unless a character is new to it.

api.sig: pub fn draw_quads(cv: graphics::Canvas, atlas: const Atlas, quads: const vector<Quad>,
api.doc: Blit laid-out quads from the sheet onto a canvas.

api.sig: pub struct Metrics
api.doc:
What the consumer measured.

⚠ `m_mono` IS A FACT ABOUT THE FACE THAT RESOLVED, not the one that was asked
for.  Requesting `DejaVuSansMono.ttf` gives a fixed-pitch face on the desktop
and a PROPORTIONAL fallback in the browser, because the browser resolves the
base name to a CSS family it does not know.  Only a measurement can tell.

api.sig: pub fn metrics_measured(wide_run: float, narrow_run: float, n: integer,
api.doc:
Build metrics from two runs the consumer measured: `n` copies of a WIDE
character and `n` copies of a NARROW one.

⚠ THE TWO RUNS ARE THE WHOLE INSTRUMENT, and one width cannot replace them.
Ten M's are ten M's in any font, so a single measurement gives the advance of
an M and nothing about whether the face is fixed-pitch.  Two same-length,
opposite-width strings answer it in one comparison.

The advance is taken from the WIDE run: under fixed pitch the two agree, and
when they do not, the wider one is the safe basis for a fits-in-the-box
question — it over-estimates rather than overflowing.

api.sig: pub fn metrics_builtin(scale: integer) -> Metrics
api.doc:
The built-in face's own metrics, so a layout written against this seam works
with no font file at all — the property `B0` exists for, carried forward.

api.sig: pub fn advance64(self: const Metrics) -> integer
api.doc: The advance in 1/64 px, as measured.

api.sig: pub fn advance(self: const Metrics) -> integer
api.doc:
The advance in whole pixels, for a caller that wants to show it.

⚠ DERIVED, NOT A SECOND FIELD.  One quantity stored twice is how two numbers
describing one distance drift apart the moment either is edited.

api.sig: pub fn height(self: const Metrics) -> integer
pub fn is_mono(self: const Metrics) -> boolean
pub fn width(self: const Metrics, s: text) -> integer
api.doc:
The ADVANCE width of `s` — what to reserve a box by.

⚠ ROUNDED UP.  The residual is a fraction of a pixel per character, and the
safe direction to spend it is outwards: an over-estimate reserves a pixel too
many and the text still fits, an under-estimate spills out of a box that was
just measured as fitting.  Exact under fixed pitch, an over-estimate
otherwise — the same reason the advance comes from the wide run.

Distinct from `text_width`, which is the built-in face's INK extent: the two
differ by the one trailing gap the ink extent leaves off, and they answer
different questions — centre by the ink, reserve by the advance.

api.sig: pub fn fits(self: const Metrics, s: text, px: integer) -> boolean
pub fn fit_text(self: const Metrics, s: text, px: integer) -> text
api.doc:
The longest prefix of `s` that fits in `px`, with ".." marking the cut.

⚠ AN UNTOUCHED STRING COMES BACK UNTOUCHED, so a caller cannot tell "fitted"
from "never measured" by looking for the marker — it appears only when
something was actually removed.

".." rather than a single "…": the ellipsis is one code point but several
bytes, and a marker whose own width is ambiguous is the wrong thing to measure
a truncation with.

⚠ CUTS BY CHARACTERS.  This shipped in B1m as `s[0..keep]`, a BYTE range given
a character count — safe, because loft snaps a byte cut outward to a character
boundary, but wrong: a non-ASCII label came back shorter than it needed to be.
B2's `take_chars` is the cure and the trap is the same one wrapping has.

api.sig: pub fn take_chars(s: text, n: integer) -> text
api.doc:
The first `n` CHARACTERS of `s`.  The cure for the trap above, and public
because every caller that slices text by a measured count needs it.

api.sig: pub fn wrap(self: const Metrics, s: text, px: integer) -> vector<text>
api.doc:
Break `s` into lines that each fit `px`, greedily, on measured advances.

⚠ A LINE ALWAYS TAKES AT LEAST ONE CHARACTER.  In a box narrower than the
narrowest glyph the alternatives are an infinite loop or dropping the text,
and a line that overflows and says so is better than either.

⚠ AND THE RESULTING TABLE IS PER TARGET.  Native measures a real TTF, the
browser measures whatever family resolved, so the same string breaks in
different places.  The invariant that travels is self-consistency: every line
here fits the box THESE metrics measured.

api.sig: pub fn align_x(self: const Metrics, line: text, bx: integer, bw: integer,
api.doc:
Where to start drawing `line` inside a box at `bx` of width `bw`.

⚠ A LINE WIDER THAN ITS BOX STARTS AT THE BOX.  Centring or right-aligning it
arithmetically would push its beginning off the left edge, where it cannot be
clipped back into view — overflow to the right is recoverable, overflow to the
left loses the start of the text.

tween.description: Property tweens in exact integer time — eleven easing curves, chains and groups

api.sig: pub enum Curve
api.doc:
Which shape the curve has.

⚠ `Back` and `Elastic` leave `[0, 1]` on purpose — they overshoot and come
back — so a consumer clamping the RESULT of an ease is undoing the effect it
asked for.  Every other curve stays inside.

api.sig: pub enum Shape
api.doc: Which direction the curve runs: slow at the start, slow at the end, or both.

api.sig: pub fn ease(c: Curve, s: Shape, t: float) -> float
api.doc:
Ease `t` — the entry point, and the three reflections of the header's rule 2.

⚠ There is no clamp HERE on purpose; every arm reads the curve through
`curve_at`, which is where the endpoints are decided.  See the header for
why in front of the reflections is the wrong side of them.

api.sig: pub fn curve_at(c: Curve, t: float) -> float
api.doc:
The curve, clamped — **the one place all thirty-three combinations get their
endpoints from.**

⚠ **Clamped, not trusted.**  `t <= 0` answers exactly 0.0 and `t >= 1`
exactly 1.0 without consulting the curve, which is what makes the endpoints
exact — including for the two curves whose textbook definitions miss them.

⚠ A `null` progress (a NaN) is neither `<= 0.0` nor `>= 1.0`, so it reaches
the curve and comes back null.  That is deliberate: an unanswerable progress
must not silently read as "finished".

api.sig: pub fn curve_in(c: Curve, t: float) -> float
api.doc:
The **In** direction of each curve, raw — the eleven definitions everything
else is reflected from.

⚠ **Public so it can be gated, not because it is the door.**  It is NOT
clamped: `curve_in(Sine, 1.0)` is `0.9999999999999999`, which is exactly the
hole `ease` exists to close.  Reach for `ease`.

api.sig: pub fn lerp(a: float, b: float, t: float) -> float
api.doc:
A linear interpolation that lands EXACTLY on both endpoints.

⚠ **`a·(1−t) + b·t`, and the other spelling is not equivalent** — see the
header: `a + (b−a)·t` answers 0.0 for `lerp(1e17, 1.0, 1.0)`.  Reach for
this one whenever an endpoint has to be hit rather than approached.

`t` outside `[0, 1]` extrapolates, which is what makes the overshooting
curves (`Back`, `Elastic`) work.

api.sig: pub struct Tween
api.doc:
One value moving from `from` to `to` over `duration` base units.

⚠ **`duration <= 0` means INSTANT, not unarmed** — it reads `to` and is
`done` immediately.  That is the opposite of `fixstep`'s `Timer`, where a
zero total means nothing is running, and it is deliberate: "move there over
no time" is a step, and a chain built from one must pass straight through
it rather than stall.

api.sig: pub fn tween_new(from: float, to: float, duration: integer,
api.doc: A tween ready to run.

api.sig: pub fn delay(self: Tween, units: integer)
api.doc:
Wait `units` before starting.

⚠ A door rather than a sixth parameter, for `fixstep`'s reason: a delay is a
case some callers have and most do not.  During the wait the tween reads
`from` and is not `done`.
