api.sig: pub fn advance(self: Tween, units: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Spend `units` of time on it, and answer how many were LEFT OVER — the time
past its end, which is what the next link of a chain must already have run
for.  Zero while it is still running.

⚠ Non-positive time is dropped rather than owed (`fixstep`'s rule 2), so a
paused consumer may call this every frame.

api.sig: pub fn progress(self: const Tween) -> float
api.doc:
How far through it is, before easing — the exact ratio `elapsed / duration`,
in `[0, 1]`.

⚠ **It reaches 1.0 and STAYS there**, which is the difference from
`fixstep`'s `timer_fraction` (documented `[0, 1)`, and 0.0 again once the
timer fires — a tween built on one would snap back to its start the instant
it finished).

api.sig: pub fn value(self: const Tween) -> float
api.doc:
What it reads right now.

⚠ Exactly `from` before it starts and exactly `to` once it has finished —
see the header for why that needs the interpolation to be written one way
and not the other.

api.sig: pub fn done(self: const Tween) -> boolean
api.doc: Has it finished?  A tween still waiting out its `delay` has not.

api.sig: pub fn rewind(self: Tween, lead: integer = 0)
api.doc: Put it back at the start, delay and all — the same tween, run again.

api.sig: pub enum Play
api.doc: How several tweens share one stream of time.

api.sig: pub struct Track
api.doc:
Several tweens driven together.

⚠ **It is a rule about time, not a scheduler** — there is no queue, no
priority and no callback.  `Chain` hands each link's leftover to the next,
which is the entire reason `advance` answers one.

api.sig: pub fn track_new(mode: Play = Play.Chain) -> Track
api.doc: An empty track.

api.sig: pub fn add(self: Track, tw: Tween)
api.doc: Add a link.  For `Chain` the order of the calls is the order they run in.

api.sig: pub fn advance(self: Track, units: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
Spend `units` on the track, and answer the leftover — the same contract one
tween has, so a track composes into a chain exactly like a tween does.

api.sig: pub fn done(self: const Track) -> boolean
api.doc: Have all its links finished?

api.sig: pub fn active(self: const Track) -> integer
api.doc: Which link is running, for `Chain` — `len(steps)` once it has finished.

api.sig: pub fn value_at(self: const Track, i: integer) -> float
api.doc:
What the link at `i` reads right now.

⚠ A door rather than making a consumer index `steps` itself, because an
out-of-range index there reads `null` and this answers `0.0`.

api.sig: pub fn rewind(self: Track)
api.doc: Put every link back at its start.

lavition_ui.description: Panel layout, hit-testing and text metrics for an in-engine editor UI: rectangles and hits, with no world, no lattice, no window and no GL.

assets.description: A game's content pack that IS a loft store — art, audio and the scenes that place them, range-read off a static file server.  No codec, no parse step, no server-side code.

api.sig: pub enum BlobKind
api.doc:
What a blob's bytes are, so a loader knows what to do with them without
sniffing the content. `Rgba` is a texture page's own pixels — premultiplied,
row-major, four bytes per texel — already decoded by the packer, so the runtime
never learns how the art was made.

api.sig: pub enum DefKind
api.doc:
Whether a definition draws or lights. A light is a placed instance like any
other, and this is what says which.

api.sig: pub struct Blob
api.doc:
Raw bytes under a key — a texture page's pixels, audio, a font, a source PNG.

One blob is the **paging unit**: `store_load_key_text` fetches the pages this
record touches and nothing else. So size a blob like an atlas page rather than
like one sprite — a store's minimum image is 8 KiB, and a finer key fetches a
page's worth either way.

api.sig: pub struct PageInfo
api.doc:
A texture page's SHAPE, and the blob key its pixels live under.

The dimensions are metadata and the pixels are bulk, so they live in different
stores. A loader that needs to know a page is 64x32 — to build UVs, to size a GL
texture, to decide what to prefetch — gets that from the boot load without
fetching a single texel.

api.sig: pub struct Cell
api.doc: One sprite's rect within a page, plus the origin a stage places it by.

api.sig: pub struct Seq
api.doc:
An animation: a run of cells laid out in one page's grid. Mirrors `stage`'s
`Sequence`, so a loader hands it straight over.

api.sig: pub struct Def
api.doc:
An object definition — GameMaker's *object*, the thing a room places.

A walk cycle is asset data and not code, so the animation table hangs off the
definition (see `anim_of`) rather than living in a game's source. A light
carries its radius, colour and power here and is placed exactly like a sprite.

api.sig: pub struct Anim
api.doc:
One row of a definition's animation table: `(action, facing) -> sequence`.
Build `an_key` as `"{def}/{action}/{facing}"`, which is what `anim_of` looks up.

api.sig: pub struct Scene
api.doc: A room: a named space that placed instances live in.

api.sig: pub struct Placed
api.doc:
A placed instance — GameMaker's *room instance*.

Definitions plus these are what a scene IS; a flat node dump cannot say that two
goblins are the same goblin. The fields mirror `stage::Place`, so loading a scene
is a copy rather than a translation.

api.sig: pub struct Pack
api.doc:
A pack's METADATA half — every collection a game reads at boot.

Binding through this container is what puts all seven collections in one file: a
keyed field shares its container's store, so one persist call writes one file and
a reader that declares the same type gets all of it. Read it WHOLE; it is small,
every part is needed from the first frame, and being a wrapper struct it cannot be
paged anyway. The bytes are the other store's job.

api.sig: pub fn new_pack() -> Pack
api.doc:
An empty pack — every collection present and none of them holding anything.

Both a packer and a loader start here: a loader declares the pack it is about to
fill, then hands it to `pack_read`.

api.sig: pub fn meta_path(base: text) -> text
api.doc:
Where a pack's metadata half lives, given the name the pack is known by.

`base` is a local path or an `http(s)://` URL — the two halves are named the same
way either side of the wire, which is what lets a game develop against a file and
ship against a CDN with only the base changed.

api.sig: pub fn blobs_path(base: text) -> text
api.doc: Where a pack's bulk half lives. Pass this to `prefetch` to page a blob out of it.

api.sig: pub fn blob_put(b: &hash<Blob[bl_key]>, key: text, kind: BlobKind,
api.doc:
Put a blob under its key, ready to be written.

Use this rather than appending: `+=` on a `&hash` parameter retypes it to a
`vector<Blob>` and the program stops compiling.

api.sig: pub fn pack_write(p: const Pack, blobs: const hash<Blob[bl_key]>,
api.doc:
Write both halves of a pack, answering whether both landed.

A pack is final by the time it ships, so this copies rather than binds: a copied
image lays each collection out in its own order, which is what makes one keyed
lookup one RUN of pages instead of a scatter — the difference between a range
read that pays for a page and one that pays for the file. Writing needs a
desktop; a browser reads packs and does not build them.

api.sig: pub fn pack_read(p: Pack, base: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
Read a pack's metadata half in full, answering whether it arrived.

Give it a pack from `new_pack`. `base` is a local path or an `http(s)://` /
`file://` URL, and that is the only thing that changes between developing against
a file and shipping against a CDN. The bytes are NOT read here — ask for those by
key, through `prefetch`, at a load or level boundary.

A URL is fetched from a source you TRUST: the image is structurally validated, so
a corrupt file is refused rather than adopted, but its contents are not
authenticated. Serve packs from your own origin, or verify the download yourself
with `store_load_url` before reading it.

api.sig: pub fn anim_of(p: const Pack, def: text, action: text, facing: integer) -> text
api.doc:
The sequence an action and a facing map to, or `""` when the definition has none.

This is the animation table's whole point: `anim_of(pack, "goblin", "walk", 2)`
answers `"goblin_walk_n"` with nothing in a game's source holding the mapping, and
an action the definition does not have answers empty rather than a plausible wrong
sequence.

api.sig: pub fn keys_near(p: const Pack, scene: text, cx: float, cy: float,
api.doc:
Every blob key a scene's instances draw from within `radius` of `(cx, cy)`.

Ask for this at a load or a level boundary, never inside a frame: a range read is
a round trip and a frame is 16 ms, so a frame that DISCOVERS it needs an asset
stutters visibly. A negative `radius` means the whole scene — what a small room
and a loading screen both want. Duplicates are dropped, because a page shared by
forty instances is still one fetch.

api.sig: pub fn prefetch(into: hash<Blob[bl_key]>, source: text,
api.doc:
Pull `keys` into `into`, and answer how many actually COST something.

`source` is `blobs_path(base)`. A key already resident is skipped, so the answer is
the number of round trips this call paid for: what a level boundary wants to log,
and what a frame must be able to assert is zero. A key the pack does not hold is
skipped too — an absent asset costs a lookup, not a record.

api.sig: pub fn layout_descriptor() -> text
api.doc:
The pack's own types, field by field, as the store records them.

Read this when the fingerprints below disagree: it names the type and the field
whose position moved, which the single number cannot. Derived by reflection from
the schema itself, so it cannot drift from it.

api.sig: pub fn layout_fingerprint() -> integer
api.doc:
One number naming this build's pack layout — compare it across targets before a
pack is read.

The struct definition IS the file layout, so a field that sits four bytes further
along on one target reads a NEIGHBOUR's value on the other, silently, and the file
looks corrupt rather than the layout looking wrong. A game that reads packs built
elsewhere should compare this once at boot and refuse rather than draw garbage.
(A 32-bit FNV-1a over `layout_descriptor`, masked at every step because an
unbounded multiply would reach loft's null.)

api.doc:
What a blob's bytes are, so a loader knows what to do with them without
sniffing the content. `Rgba` is a texture page's own pixels — premultiplied,
row-major, four bytes per texel — already decoded by the packer, so the runtime
never learns how the art was made.

api.doc:
Whether a definition draws or lights. A light is a placed instance like any
other, and this is what says which.

api.sig: pub struct Cell
api.doc:
One sprite's rect within a page, plus the origin a stage places it by.

`ce_proxy` is the collision proxy DERIVED from this cell's own alpha at pack

derived one — a pack built before proxies, or a cell with no opaque texels —
and an empty proxy hits nothing, so a consumer that finds one absent falls back
to the cell rect rather than colliding with everything.

api.sig: pub struct Seq
api.doc:
An animation: a run of cells laid out in one page's grid. Mirrors `stage`'s
`Sequence`, so a loader hands it straight over.

api.sig: pub struct Def
api.doc:
An object definition — GameMaker's *object*, the thing a room places.

A walk cycle is asset data and not code, so the animation table hangs off the

api.doc:
One row of a definition's animation table: `(action, facing) -> sequence`.
Build `an_key` as `"{def}/{action}/{facing}"`, which is what `anim_of` looks up.

api.sig: pub struct Scene
api.doc: A room: a named space that placed instances live in.

api.sig: pub struct Placed
api.doc:
A placed instance — GameMaker's *room instance*.

Definitions plus these are what a scene IS; a flat node dump cannot say that two

A pack's METADATA half — every collection a game reads at boot.

api.sig: pub fn new_pack() -> Pack
api.doc:
An empty pack — every collection present and none of them holding anything.

Both a packer and a loader start here: a loader declares the pack it is about to
fill, then hands it to `pack_read`.

api.sig: pub fn meta_path(base: text) -> text
api.doc:
Where a pack's metadata half lives, given the name the pack is known by.

`base` is a local path or an `http(s)://` URL — the two halves are named the same
way either side of the wire, which is what lets a game develop against a file and
ship against a CDN with only the base changed.

api.sig: pub fn blobs_path(base: text) -> text
api.doc: Where a pack's bulk half lives. Pass this to `prefetch` to page a blob out of it.

api.sig: pub fn blob_put(b: &hash<Blob[bl_key]>, key: text, kind: BlobKind,
api.doc:
Put a blob under its key, ready to be written.

Use this rather than appending: `+=` on a `&hash` parameter retypes it to a
`vector<Blob>` and the program stops compiling.

api.sig: pub fn pack_write(p: const Pack, blobs: const hash<Blob[bl_key]>,
api.doc:
Write both halves of a pack, answering whether both landed.

A pack is final by the time it ships, so this copies rather than binds: a copied
image lays each collection out in its own order, which is what makes one keyed
lookup one RUN of pages instead of a scatter — the difference between a range
read that pays for a page and one that pays for the file. Writing needs a
desktop; a browser reads packs and does not build them.

api.sig: pub fn pack_read(p: Pack, base: text) -> boolean
api.doc:
Read a pack's metadata half in full, answering whether it arrived.

Give it a pack from `new_pack`. `base` is a local path or an `http(s)://` /
`file://` URL, and that is the only thing that changes between developing against
a file and shipping against a CDN. The bytes are NOT read here — ask for those by
key, through `prefetch`, at a load or level boundary.

A URL is fetched from a source you TRUST: the image is structurally validated, so
a corrupt file is refused rather than adopted, but its contents are not
authenticated. Serve packs from your own origin, or verify the download yourself
with `store_load_url` before reading it.

api.sig: pub fn anim_of(p: const Pack, def: text, action: text, facing: integer) -> text
api.doc:
The sequence an action and a facing map to, or `""` when the definition has none.

This is the animation table's whole point: `anim_of(pack, "goblin", "walk", 2)`
answers `"goblin_walk_n"` with nothing in a game's source holding the mapping, and
an action the definition does not have answers empty rather than a plausible wrong
sequence.

api.sig: pub fn keys_near(p: const Pack, scene: text, cx: float, cy: float,
api.doc:
Every blob key a scene's instances draw from within `radius` of `(cx, cy)`.

Ask for this at a load or a level boundary, never inside a frame: a range read is
a round trip and a frame is 16 ms, so a frame that DISCOVERS it needs an asset
stutters visibly. A negative `radius` means the whole scene — what a small room
and a loading screen both want. Duplicates are dropped, because a page shared by
forty instances is still one fetch.

api.sig: pub fn prefetch(into: hash<Blob[bl_key]>, source: text,
api.doc:
Pull `keys` into `into`, and answer how many actually COST something.

`source` is `blobs_path(base)`. A key already resident is skipped, so the answer is
the number of round trips this call paid for: what a level boundary wants to log,
and what a frame must be able to assert is zero. A key the pack does not hold is
skipped too — an absent asset costs a lookup, not a record.

api.sig: pub fn opaque_texels(ot_px: const vector<u8>, ot_page: const PageInfo,
api.doc:
How many texels of this cell are opaque — the thing a proxy stands for, and the
denominator of `proxy_overshoot`.

api.sig: pub fn cell_proxy(c: const Cell, page: const PageInfo, px: const vector<u8>,
api.doc:
Derive `c`'s collision proxy from the page's own alpha, in cell-local
coordinates.

Banded on the TIGHTER axis: the derivation runs both ways and keeps the smaller
total area. 17 of the 36 corpus sprites band better by column than by row, so
choosing per sprite rather than fixing an axis takes the median overshoot from
+29.2 % to +22.8 % — for the cost of running a pass twice at pack time, which
is a cost nothing at runtime pays.

A cell with no opaque texels derives an EMPTY proxy, and an empty proxy hits
nothing. That is the answer a fully transparent cell should give; a single box
around it would collide with whatever stood there.

api.sig: pub fn proxy_overshoot(po_boxes: const vector<shapes::Rect>, po_solid: integer) -> float
api.doc:
How much bigger a derived proxy is than the art it stands for.

The number F7 gates on: `<= 1.0` is at most twice the art. Reported per sprite
rather than asserted in aggregate, because one adversarial shape — three thin
diagonal arrows — misses the bound at every band count, and a bound nothing can
violate is not a bound.

api.sig: pub fn layout_descriptor() -> text
api.doc:
The pack's own types, field by field, as the store records them.

Read this when the fingerprints below disagree: it names the type and the field
whose position moved, which the single number cannot. Derived by reflection from
the schema itself, so it cannot drift from it.

api.sig: pub fn layout_fingerprint() -> integer
api.doc:
One number naming this build's pack layout — compare it across targets before a
pack is read.

The struct definition IS the file layout, so a field that sits four bytes further
along on one target reads a NEIGHBOUR's value on the other, silently, and the file
looks corrupt rather than the layout looking wrong. A game that reads packs built
elsewhere should compare this once at boot and refuse rather than draw garbage.
(A 32-bit FNV-1a over `layout_descriptor`, masked at every step because an
unbounded multiply would reach loft's null.)

drawing.description: Render a .draw scene — a sprite authored as lines of text — pixel-identically to the Python renderer it replaces

api.sig: pub enum PaintKind
api.doc: How a mark is filled, if it is filled at all.

api.sig: pub struct Paint
api.doc:
A mark's fill descriptor.

`Stroked` is the absence of a fill, not a fill of nothing: it is what sends a
`Poly` down the pen path instead of the polygon path, and the two produce
completely different pictures from the same points.

api.sig: pub enum OpKind
api.doc: What an op does.

api.sig: pub struct Op
api.doc:
One entry in the ordered draw program.

⚠ `pts` are FRACTIONS of the paper (0..1, origin top-left, y down), never
pixels.  The scale to pixels happens once, at the raster call, because the
paper size is a property of the scene and the supersample factor is a
property of the renderer — neither belongs in a parsed mark.

api.sig: pub struct Elem
api.doc: A named group of marks and the box they cover, in paper fractions.

api.sig: pub struct Landmark
api.doc: A `landmark <name> = <value>` line.

api.sig: pub struct Sketch
api.doc:
A parsed scene: the paper, the ordered draw program, and everything the
parser could measure or could not accept.

⚠ NOT called `Scene`: `mesh3d::Scene` owns that name and `graphics` depends on
mesh3d, so the collision is a hard error — the same trap `graphics::Coord`
hit with `Point`.  Reach for `Sketch` in `.draw` code and the 3-D names stay
where they belong.

api.sig: pub fn grey(gl: float) -> integer
api.doc:
A grey level in 0..1 as an opaque colour, rounded HALF TO EVEN.

Python's `round` is half-to-even and `draw.py` uses it here, so `fill=0.5`
is 128 and not 127 — a difference of one level that no eye would find and a
byte diff would.

api.sig: pub struct PointList
api.doc: Every `(x,y)` on a line, with the two suffixes a point may carry.

api.sig: pub fn read_points(s: text) -> PointList
api.doc:
`\(\s*(n)\s*,\s*(n)\s*\)\s*(~?)\s*(?:@\s*(n))?`, found repeatedly along the line.

Scanning for points rather than splitting the line is what lets the same
grammar carry options: `rgb=140,104,62` has no parentheses, so it is not a
point, and no separator has to be agreed between the two.

api.sig: pub fn circle_pts(cx: float, cy: float, r: float, n: integer, flat: float,
api.doc:
The outline of a `Circle`, as `draw.py` builds it: `n` segments round the
centre with the FIRST point repeated at the end, so the polygon closes
itself and Pillow adds no edge of its own.

`flat` squashes the vertical radius; the `W/H` factor keeps the circle round
on non-square paper, since the coordinates are fractions of each axis.

api.sig: pub fn smooth_applies(pts: const vector<raster::Pt>, flags: const vector<boolean>) -> boolean
api.doc:
Does this outline curve at all?  Fewer than three points, or no `~`, and the
control points ARE the polyline — which is what keeps a plain `Poly`
unchanged.

api.sig: pub fn smooth_pts(pts: const vector<raster::Pt>, flags: const vector<boolean>,
api.doc:
Expand control points to a dense polyline.

A point flagged `~` curves (its tangent is half the neighbour chord); a
corner uses the segment chord, which makes that segment exactly straight.  So
one outline mixes straight runs and curves, and a segment between two corners
is a line however many `~` the rest of the outline has.

api.sig: pub fn smooth_vals(vals: const vector<float>, closed: boolean) -> vector<float>
api.doc: The per-point widths carried across the same expansion, interpolated linearly.

api.sig: pub fn parse_scene(src: text) -> Sketch
api.doc:
Parse a whole `.draw` source.

The command order below is `draw.py`'s, and it is not alphabetical or
tidy — `Circle` is tried before `Poly`, `Line` last of all.  Keep it: a
grammar this loose is defined by the order its alternatives are tried in,
and re-sorting it silently re-reads lines that sit in two alternatives.

api.sig: pub fn render(sc: const Sketch) -> graphics::Canvas
api.doc:
Draw a parsed scene: at `SUPERSAMPLE`x, then resampled down with Lanczos.

A transparent background renders on transparent pixels so the resample
anti-aliases edges against ALPHA rather than against white — which is what
makes the result a sprite that can be composited over anything, with no
colour-key hack.

api.sig: pub fn render_file(src: text, out: text) -> Sketch
api.doc:
Render a `.draw` file to a PNG, answering the parsed scene so the caller can
report what it could not accept.

api.sig: pub struct Pt
api.doc:
A point in canvas pixels, before Pillow truncates it to a whole pixel.

The truncation is `(int)` on a C double — toward ZERO, so `-0.4` lands on 0
and not on -1.  Keep coordinates fractional right up to the rasteriser and
the port and the oracle round the same way.

api.sig: pub fn pt(px: float, py: float) -> Pt
api.doc: Build a point without spelling the field names.

api.sig: pub fn round_up(ru_v: float) -> integer
api.doc:
`ROUND_UP` from `Draw.c` — half AWAY from zero.

Not `floor(f + 0.5)`: the sign lives outside, so the negative side mirrors
the positive one exactly (`ROUND_UP(-0.5)` is -1, not 0).

api.sig: pub fn round_down(rd_v: float) -> integer
api.doc:
`ROUND_DOWN` from `Draw.c` — `ceil(f - 0.5)`, mirrored about zero.

The mirroring is the whole subtlety: `ROUND_DOWN(-0.45)` is **0**, because
the `ceil` runs on `|f| - 0.5` and the sign is applied afterwards.  Take the
obvious `ceil(-0.95)` instead and a span that should end on column 0 ends on
column -1, which clips away and draws nothing.

api.sig: pub fn fill_poly(cv: graphics::Canvas, pts: const vector<Pt>, ink: integer)
api.doc:
Fill a polygon the way `ImageDraw.polygon(pts, fill=…)` does.

The outline closes itself only when the last point is not already the first —
a circle handed in with its start repeated gets no extra edge, which is how
`draw.py` passes one.

api.sig: pub fn wide_line(cv: graphics::Canvas, wx0: float, wy0: float, wx1: float, wy1: float,
api.doc:
One thick segment, the way `ImageDraw.line(…, width=w)` draws it for `w > 1`.

Pillow does not stroke — it builds a four-cornered quad around the segment
and fills that, with the two half-widths rounded APART (`ROUND_UP` one side,
`ROUND_DOWN` the other) so an even width still lands on whole pixels.  A
polyline is therefore a series of independent quads with no joins, and the
overlap at a bend is what rounds the corner.

api.sig: pub fn thin_line(cv: graphics::Canvas, pts: const vector<Pt>, ink: integer)
api.doc:
`line32` from `Draw.c` — Bresenham, and it stops one pixel SHORT of the end.

`draw_lines` puts that missing pixel back after the last segment, which is
why this is a polyline call rather than a segment one: split it into
segments and each one grows a pixel Pillow never drew.

api.sig: pub struct Scan
api.doc:
A parse position and what was read there.

A scan either lands (`ok`) or does not, and the caller needs BOTH the value
and where to carry on from, so every reader answers all three at once.

api.sig: pub fn scan_fail() -> Scan
pub fn is_digit(b: integer) -> boolean
pub fn is_word_byte(b: integer) -> boolean
api.doc: A regex `\w`: letters, digits and underscore.

api.sig: pub fn is_space_byte(b: integer) -> boolean
api.doc: A regex `\s`: space, tab, and the line endings a stray `\r` leaves behind.

api.sig: pub fn at(s: text, i: integer) -> integer
api.doc:
The byte at `i`, or -1 past either end — a value no byte can take, so a
caller never has to bound-check before asking.

api.sig: pub fn lower_byte(b: integer) -> integer
api.doc: ASCII lowercase of one byte.

api.sig: pub fn skip_space(s: text, i: integer) -> integer
api.doc: Past any run of spaces starting at `i`.

api.sig: pub fn matches_at(s: text, i: integer, word: text) -> boolean
api.doc: Does `s` carry `word` at byte `i`, ignoring case?  (`word` must be lowercase.)

api.sig: pub fn word_boundary(s: text, i: integer) -> boolean
api.doc: A regex `\b` before byte `i`: position 0, or a non-word byte to the left.

api.sig: pub fn read_number(s: text, i: integer) -> Scan
api.doc:
A regex `([-\d.]+)` — a run of digits, dots and minus signs, read as a number.

The character class is what `draw.py` writes, so this is deliberately loose:
the run is taken first and converted second, and a run that is not a number
fails the scan rather than being silently read as zero.

api.sig: pub fn read_unsigned(s: text, i: integer) -> Scan
api.doc: A regex `([\d.]+)` — digits and dots, no sign.

api.sig: pub fn read_uint(s: text, i: integer) -> Scan
api.doc: A regex `(\d+)` — digits only.

api.sig: pub fn find_option(s: text, key: text) -> Scan
api.doc:
The first `\b<key>\s*=\s*` on the line, answering where its VALUE starts.

This is the shape every option regex in `draw.py` opens with, and the
word-boundary is load-bearing rather than decorative: without it `w=` would
also be found inside `w2=`, which is a different option with a different
meaning.  `key` must be lowercase; the match is not.

api.sig: pub fn find_word_from(s: text, word: text, start: integer) -> Scan
api.doc:
The first occurrence of a lowercase `word` at or after `start`, ignoring case
— a regex literal with no boundary condition, which is what `Circle` and
`Line` open with.

The `start` is what makes a failed parse behave like `re.search`: a command
whose first occurrence does not parse is retried from the NEXT one rather
than given up on.
